findings.source: gov.br Secom Feb 2025 https://www.gov.br/secom/pt-br/acompanhe-a-secom/noticias/2025/02/governo-federal-e-embraer-anunciam-r-20-bilhoes-em-investimentos-no-brasil-ate-2030 (search excerpt); Embraer FQ4 2020 call 19 Mar 2021 p420
findings.quote: securing more than $1 billion in finance from different sources, such as BNDES, U.S. EXIM private and public banks (Embraer, 2021)
findings.unit: BRL bn investment plan to 2030 / BRL bn BNDES financing (Republic)
findings.use_in_model: A Brazilian state backstop makes a post-exit Embraer entry more plausible. It is also the only way the 35% JV capex share could be funded.

findings.topic: Boeing's own view of the field
findings.claim: Boeing's 10-K list of share-seeking rivals narrowed from 'Airbus, Embraer and Bombardier, and other entrants from Russia, China and Japan' (FY2012-17), to 'Airbus and other entrants from Russia, China and Japan' (FY2018-FY2020), to 'Airbus and entrants from China' (FY2022-FY2024).
findings.quote: We face aggressive international competitors who are intent on increasing their market share, such as Airbus and entrants from China. (FY2024 10-K)
findings.unit: named entrant countries (Russia, China, Japan -> China)
findings.direction: toward launch (an exit cedes to Airbus and China)
findings.use_in_model: By Boeing's own account the geopolitical stake in an exit is COMAC, not Embraer. Tie any doctrine or geopolitical premium to modelled COMAC share in the Do Nothing branch.

findings.topic: Failed entrant: Mitsubishi SpaceJet
findings.claim: Japan's state-supported entrant failed. Mitsubishi formally paused the SpaceJet in 2020 (Pratt & Whitney signed a contract recognising the pause), and analysts noted in 2021 that Bombardier and Mitsubishi had dropped out, leaving only Embraer below 110 seats. The programme was cancelled in Feb 2023 after about ¥1 trillion spent (from memory).
findings.source: Repo P-1939 (RTX 10-K FY2020 p1451); Embraer FQ4 2020 call 19 Mar 2021 p426; cancellation and cost from memory
findings.quote: Bombardier and Mitsubishi essentially dropping out of the new aircraft production market. So now really in RJs or at least up to 110 seats, it's only Embraer (Spingarn, Credit Suisse)
findings.use_in_model: Entry barriers are very high even with state support. A post-exit entrant (Embraer or others) should carry a high failure probability.

findings.topic: Russian entrant constrained by US export controls
findings.claim: After the 2022 invasion Pratt & Whitney stopped shipping engines to Irkut, the MC-21's maker, which cut off its Western GTF. The MC-21 was then re-engined with Russian powerplants (from memory; its 2025-26 status was not verified this session).
findings.source: Repo P-0098 (RTX Q1 2022 call, Hayes, p517); MC-21 re-engining from memory
findings.quote: at Pratt, we're not shipping engines to Irkut.
findings.direction: toward Do Nothing (the US has non-Boeing levers against adversary entrants)
findings.use_in_model: Washington can slow adversary entrants through export controls on engines and systems, so a Boeing product is not the only US lever. This lowers the 'cede to enemies' premium somewhat.

findings.topic: Boeing's Brazil defence history
findings.claim: Boeing's 2012 Embraer agreements were a localisation effort for its F/A-18 bid in Brazil's 36-fighter competition ('a good shot in Brazil'). Brazil chose Saab's Gripen in Dec 2013, a decision widely reported as linked to the NSA spying revelations (from memory). Boeing referred to 'the Brazilian's decision' in Apr 2014.
findings.source: Repo B-0601 (FQ1 2012 call, 25 Apr 2012, Transcripts p2404); Boeing shareholder call 22 May 2013 p2146; FQ1 2014 call 23 Apr 2014 p2003; Gripen and NSA context from memory
findings.quote: So when you say Embraer, you're talking about some localization efforts we've got in Brazil... I think we have a good shot in Brazil.
findings.use_in_model: US-Brazil politics have cost Boeing before. Brazilian state choices follow sovereignty and local content more than alliance. Any Brazil-linked fps route carries political risk in both directions.

findings.topic: Boeing used trade law against state-backed entrants
findings.claim: Boeing framed the WTO launch-aid ruling against Airbus as a precedent against emerging competitors from Canada, Brazil, China and Russia, using trade law rather than product to deter entrants.
findings.source: Repo B-0271 / BX-0657 (McNerney, FQ2 2010 call, 28 Jul 2010, Transcripts p2708)
findings.quote: it sets the precedent for emerging competitors from Canada, Brazil, China, Russia and others, who want to enter the market.
findings.use_in_model: Boeing's established lever against new entrants is Washington (trade cases, tariffs), not only new products. Model DC as a lever Boeing can pull, not just as pressure on Boeing.

findings.topic: Analyst framing of Boeing as the US trade champion
findings.claim: BofA's Kristine Liwag described the large-aircraft industry as still a duopoly and Boeing as historically 'the tip of the trade spear' for the US in a net-exporting industry, and asked Embraer about a larger aircraft. Embraer said it had no decision.
findings.source: Embraer FQ1 2025 call 6 May 2025 (Embraer Transcripts p104-105)
findings.quote: strategically, historically, Boeing was the tip of the trade spear for the U.S. and all this tariff stuff is a reminder that this is a net exporting industry for the U.S.
findings.use_in_model: An analyst (sell-side) view that supports a US-national-interest term. This is opinion, so weight it below behavioural evidence.

findings.topic: Boeing 2026 openness to partner models
findings.claim: Ortberg (Jul 2026) said the next airplane may involve 'different kind of business partnerships, different type of ventures'. CFO Malave (Mar 2026) said Boeing will develop a new programme 'at the right time' but that the market, the technology and Boeing are not ready. Neither named Embraer.
findings.source: Boeing FQ2 2026 call 28 Jul 2026 (Transcript Digest (4) p45); Company Conference 17 Mar 2026 p100
findings.quote: it could require different kind of business partnerships, different type of ventures, certainly a different level of engagement with our supply chain (Ortberg); it's unrealistic to say that we'll never develop a new program, we will, at the right time (Malave)
findings.direction: toward launch (via a partner or JV)
findings.use_in_model: Management does not frame an exit. A partner-financed fps variant is consistent with stated intent, but Embraer's capacity limits (see the financial-capacity finding) point to supplier or sovereign partners rather than Embraer alone.

findings.topic: Embraer positions itself alongside COMAC in China
findings.claim: The E190-E2 was certified in China in 2022, and Embraer markets the E2 as complementary to COMAC's ARJ21/C909 and C919. Embraer sells into both US and Chinese markets.
findings.source: Embraer FQ4 2022 call 10 Mar 2023 p300; FQ2 2023 call 14 Aug 2023 p276; FQ4 2024 call 27 Feb 2025 p144
findings.quote: the benefit of the E2 family is that it is truly complementary to the Chinese products (Meijer, Feb 2025)
findings.use_in_model: Embraer is commercially multi-aligned. In a post-exit world it could complement COMAC rather than counter it, so it is not a substitute for a US-led narrowbody in a 'contain China' framing.

findings.topic: Boeing's Brazil engineering presence after the JV
findings.claim: A Brazilian journalist on Embraer's Nov 2024 call said Boeing's late-2024 layoffs included staff at its São José dos Campos office (Boeing's Brazil engineering presence, which sits next to Embraer's headquarters). Embraer declined to comment beyond saying it follows its own strategy.
findings.source: Embraer FQ3 2024 call 8 Nov 2024 (Embraer Transcripts p200-201); the claim is the journalist's, not verified
findings.quote: They are laying off many employees, including people from Sao Jose dos Campos office.
findings.direction: toward Do Nothing (Boeing retreats from Brazil under cost pressure)
findings.use_in_model: A weak signal that Boeing cuts foreign engineering footprint in downturns regardless of political symbolism. Verify before use.

research.summary:
Scope and limits. Most findings come from the repo: Boeing 10-Ks, the 2006-2025 transcripts, the 2026 Transcript Digest, the Embraer and Rolls-Royce transcripts, the Airbus FY2025 board report as quoted in airbus/evidence.jsonl, and franchise_research.json, which cites its own URLs. The shared web-search budget was already used up when I started, and www.wto.org and en.wikipedia.org did not resolve, so I could not run any web searches. Items not in the repo are marked 'model knowledge, not verified this session'. Those dated 2025 are low confidence and need checking.

What the record shows about the 'bill cut'.
(1) Governments outside the US routinely pay for the launch itself. Under the 1992 US-EC deal, Airbus could get state loans covering up to 33% of development. The A380 and A350 got roughly EUR 3.3-3.7B each. Quebec paid US$1B for 49.5% of the CSeries, about 17% of its roughly $6B cost, and still holds 25% of Airbus Canada. Chinese state support for COMAC (US$49-72B) exceeds the C919's whole development cost. The UK carries about 29% of Rolls-Royce's gross R&D.
(2) The US pays mostly through states, tax and demand, not launch money. Washington's 2003 package for the 787 and its 2013 extension for the 777X were $3.2B and $8.7B on paper. At 10.5% they are worth only about $1.3-1.5B each in present value. South Carolina's cash grants were $346M. The CARES Act gave Boeing a $1.175B tax benefit. In 2025-26 the administration acted as Boeing's sales agent: the Qatar and other trade-deal orders, and a 200-aircraft China commitment that reopened the Chinese market to Boeing narrowbodies.
(3) Federal rescues of the Lockheed, Chrysler and GM kind were crisis loans to prevent a collapse, not launch funding. The one direct federal airliner launch, the SST, was cancelled by Congress in 1971 despite mass Boeing layoffs.

Constraints that shrink the cut.
- Retaliation: the WTO let the EU impose $3.99B a year of tariffs over a single Washington tax break.
- Boeing's own pledge: in 2021 it endorsed the US-EU rule that all future support must be 'on market terms', and in 2020 it gave up the Washington tax break.
- Strings: support tends to come with job commitments and royalties (P&W Canada paid $867M to settle Canadian aid) or equity and golden-share conditions (2025: Intel, US Steel, MP Materials; unverified).
- Boeing's own record: it avoided state money in 2020 ($25B of bonds) and 2024 ($24B of equity).

Counter-evidence that politics does not change Boeing's choices:
- It consolidated 787 production in South Carolina in 2020, despite Washington's incentives.
- It lost the 2017 CSeries trade case 4-0 at the ITC. The case pushed the CSeries to Airbus and cost Boeing a Canadian Super Hornet buy (memory).
- Ex-Im Bank financing lapsed in 2015 and the bank lacked a quorum until 2019, despite Boeing's lobbying.
- Governments let Lockheed (1981), Fokker (1996), Douglas (1997), Rolls-Royce in narrowbody engines (2012), Bombardier (2020) and Mitsubishi (2023) leave. My inference: none of them was a duopolist with about 40% of a market, and in a Boeing exit no US champion would remain, so the political stakes would be higher than in any precedent.

How this could move the fps decision (inference). A realistic US 'bill cut' is worth about $1-3B in present value at 10.5%:
- a state siting package won through a site competition: about $1.3-2B;
- federal R&D and tax help: a few hundred million;
- demand diplomacy: affects volume, not cost.
That is 2-5% of a $60-65B programme. An Airbus-style 33% loan (about $20B gross) is effectively closed to Boeing by its own 'market terms' pledge, and would invite matching support for Airbus's NGSA. A $1-3B cut closes a quarter to three quarters of the roughly $4B gap at 10.5%. It does not clear the $1B business-case test on its own, but it could decide the $1B tie rule. At 8.1% it adds to an fps that already beats Do Nothing. It fits inside the Board's $2B 'doctrine premium' cap (H8) and should be entered there, as a separate, evidenced line, net of a retaliation haircut. It should not be treated as a reason to launch on its own.

findings.topic: WTO countermeasure awards (both sides)
findings.claim: The WTO authorised the US (October 2019) to impose about $7.5B a year of tariffs on EU goods over eight instances of Airbus launch aid. It authorised the EU (October 2020) to impose about $3.99B a year over a Washington State tax incentive used by Boeing. Each side then put 15% tariffs on the other's aircraft.
findings.source: Boeing 10-K FY2020 p.1369 (/home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Boeing 10ks.zip -> Boeing 10ks.pdf); repo ids B-2509, B-1761
findings.quote: the WTO authorized the EU to impose approximately $3.99 billion in annual tariffs on U.S. products in connection with a tax incentive used by Boeing in Washington state that has since been repealed
findings.direction: toward Do Nothing (makes any non-market government support for the fps costly)
findings.use_in_model: Any government 'bill cut' that is not on market terms should carry a retaliation cost: EU tariffs on Boeing deliveries, or licence for a matching Airbus NGSA subsidy. A single state tax break produced an award of about $4B a year.

findings.topic: Boeing gave up its Washington tax break to end EU tariffs
findings.claim: The Washington aerospace business-and-occupation (B&O) tax preference behind the EU award was repealed, and Boeing itself sought the repeal. From model knowledge: Boeing asked the legislature in February 2020 and the repeal took effect on 1 April 2020. The 2013 extension it cancelled had been valued at about $8.7B through 2040. Boeing traded a state subsidy for tariff-free access to European customers.
findings.source: Boeing 10-K FY2020 p.1369 (repo B-1761) for the repeal; the timing and the $8.7B value are model knowledge, not verified this session (no web access)
findings.quote: a tax incentive used by Boeing in Washington state that has since been repealed
findings.use_in_model: Shows that state bill cuts can be reversed and that Boeing will give them up for market access. Apply a haircut or a reversal probability to any assumed state incentive in the fps case.

findings.topic: Washington 2003 incentives for the 787: share of programme cost
findings.claim: Washington's 2003 package to land 787 final assembly was about $3.2B over 20 years (model knowledge). My calculation: spread evenly over 2005-2024 it is worth about $1.32B in 2004 at 10.5% ($1.56B at 8.1%). That is about 16% of the roughly $20B 787 development cost on paper, and about 7% in present value.
findings.source: $3.2B: model knowledge (Washington 2003 aerospace tax legislation), not verified this session. 787 development of about $20B: franchise_research.json, citing Leeham 19 Oct 2015 https://leehamnews.com/2015/10/19/do-the-boeing-787-sums-add-up/. PV: own calculation
findings.number: 3.2 nominal; 1.32 PV at 10.5%; ~7% of development in PV
findings.use_in_model: Benchmark for a US state 'bill cut' on a clean sheet: about $1.3-1.6B of present value, or about 2-2.5% of a $60-65B fps. Enter it in the doctrine-premium line (H8), not in the base case.

findings.topic: 777X site auction (2013): Boeing used DC-style pressure on states and unions
findings.claim: In December 2013 Boeing ran a site competition for the 777X involving more than a dozen states. It kept the wing and final assembly in Puget Sound after Washington extended its incentives (about $8.7B, 2024-2040, memory). The IAM also agreed a contract to 2024 that moved workers from defined-benefit to defined-contribution pensions. My calculation: the extension was worth about $1.47B in 2013 at 10.5% ($2.13B at 8.1%).
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcripts from 2006-2025_Compressed.pdf p.2056 (Company Conference Presentation, 4 Dec 2013) and p.1952 (Shareholder/Analyst Call, 21 May 2014); $8.7B is model knowledge; PV is own calculation
findings.quote: we're in the middle of a site competition. And as you know, yes, more than 1 dozen states are involved in that deliberate process right now
findings.use_in_model: An fps launch would itself trigger a site competition. Expect about $1.5-2B of present value plus labour concessions. This lowers the effective fps bill, and it is a lever that exists only if Boeing launches.

findings.topic: South Carolina cash grants for the 787
findings.claim: Boeing received $346M in cash grants from South Carolina between 2010 and 2016 for its operations there, amortised through 2052. That is about 1.7% of the roughly $20B 787 development cost, or about $0.24B in 2009 present value at 10.5%. From model knowledge, the full 2009 South Carolina package including bonds and tax relief was nearer $0.9B (low confidence).
findings.source: Boeing 10-K FY2024 p.2257 and FY2023 p.382 (Government Assistance note), /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Boeing 10ks.zip
findings.quote: Between 2010 and 2016, we received cash grants totaling $ 346 related to our investment in operations in South Carolina.
findings.use_in_model: Floor for a second-state bill cut: a few hundred million dollars, about 0.5% of an fps. Competing states set the price, not federal policy.

findings.topic: Incentives did not hold Boeing's footprint: 787 moved out of Everett
findings.claim: In 2020 Boeing consolidated all 787 production in South Carolina, taking it out of Washington despite the state's 2003 incentives for the 787. It said the move 'did not have a significant financial impact on the program'. In 2009 it had placed the second line in Charleston partly to diversify away from the Puget Sound union.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcripts from 2006-2025_Compressed.pdf p.803 (FQ3 2020 Earnings Call, 28 Oct 2020); Boeing 10-K FY2020 p.1375; repo B-0218 (FQ3 2009 call p.2792)
findings.quote: we made the decision to consolidate the 787 production in South Carolina by mid-'21
findings.use_in_model: Counter-evidence: political pressure over jobs and past subsidies did not override Boeing's footprint economics. Do not assume jobs politics forces a launch.

findings.topic: Boeing used Washington trade law against a narrowbody rival: CSeries 2017
findings.claim: Boeing petitioned the Commerce Department in 2017 against Bombardier's CSeries, accusing it of 'illegal subsidies' and 'dumping'. It kept the case going after Airbus took control and announced an Alabama line. Commerce set combined duties of about 292% (model knowledge: final CVD about 212% plus AD about 80%, December 2017). The ITC then voted 4-0 in January 2018 that there was no injury, and Boeing lost. Meanwhile Airbus took 50.01% of the CSeries for no cash.
findings.source: Repo BX-1105 and B-1309 (FQ3 2017 call, 25 Oct 2017, p.1366) and B-1339 (FQ4 2017 call, 31 Jan 2018, p.1331), in /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/; duty rates and ITC vote are model knowledge; Airbus deal from franchise_research.json, citing CNBC 16 Oct 2017 https://www.cnbc.com/2017/10/16/airbus-teams-up-with-bombardier-on-c-series-program.html
findings.quote: Bombardier's actions on the C Series, where they have received illegal subsidies and they've exhibited dumping behavior, those will be evaluated by the Department of Commerce
findings.number: ~292 (combined duty, memory); 0-4 ITC vote (memory); 50.01% for C$1
findings.use_in_model: Boeing does use DC against narrowbody rivals, but trade remedies failed and pushed the rival to Airbus. Do not count trade action as a substitute for a product. Under Do Nothing, Boeing would have no product with which to defend the segment.

findings.topic: Cost of the CSeries fight in Canada
findings.claim: From model knowledge: during the trade case, Canada dropped its plan to buy 18 interim Boeing Super Hornets (about US$5B) in December 2017 and bought used Australian F/A-18s instead. Canada later chose the F-35. Using DC against an ally had a cost in Boeing's defence business.
findings.source: Model knowledge, not verified this session (web search budget used up)
findings.use_in_model: Political levers have side costs. If the fps case uses DC trade pressure on Airbus or COMAC, add a cost for retaliation by allied buyers.

findings.topic: Quebec and Canada: share of the CSeries bill
findings.claim: Quebec put in US$1B for 49.5% of the CSeries (2015-16). On a roughly $6B programme that is about 17% of development. From model knowledge, Ottawa added C$372.5M of repayable loans in 2017, mostly for the Global 7000. Quebec stayed in after Bombardier sold out in February 2020 for $591M. At end-2025, Airbus held 75% of Airbus Canada and Investissement Quebec 25%, which Airbus can redeem in 2035.
findings.source: franchise_research.json, CSeries finding citing Leeham 29 Oct 2015 https://leehamnews.com/2015/10/29/bombardier-3-2bn-charge-1bn-from-quebec/; Airbus Board Report FY2025 p.20 (repo A-0265, /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/airbus/evidence.jsonl); federal loan is model knowledge
findings.quote: At the end of 2025, the Airbus Canada shareholding structure was 75% Airbus and 25% IQ, with the IQ stake being redeemable by Airbus in 2035.
findings.use_in_model: A sub-national government carried about one sixth of a narrowbody bill and still could not prevent its champion's exit. On a $60-65B fps, a 17% share would be about $10-11B, but no US precedent exists for that scale.

findings.topic: 1992 US-EC Large Civil Aircraft Agreement: the old ceiling on state bills
findings.claim: From model knowledge: the 1992 agreement capped direct government support at 33% of a programme's development cost, repayable with interest at no less than the government's cost of borrowing within 17 years. It capped indirect support at 3% of the industry's civil aircraft turnover. The US abandoned the agreement when it filed the WTO case in 2004.
findings.source: Model knowledge (US-EC Agreement on Trade in Large Civil Aircraft, July 1992), not verified this session
findings.unit: % of development cost; % of LCA turnover
findings.use_in_model: The historical upper bound the US tolerated for a state bill cut, though for Airbus, not Boeing. On the fps that would be about $20-21B gross. The repayable loan's subsidy element is far smaller than the gross: my inference is roughly a quarter to a third of it.

findings.topic: Airbus repayable launch investment by programme
findings.claim: From model knowledge: the WTO case (DS316) covered member-state financing for the A300, A310, A320, A330/A340 and A380. A380 member-state financing was about EUR 3.3-3.7B, about one third of the A380's roughly EUR 11-12B development cost. The A350 XWB received about EUR 3.3B of repayable launch investment from France, Germany, Spain and the UK, about 22-30% of its EUR 11-15B cost. In 2010-11 the WTO found every instance of launch aid challenged by the US to be a subsidy.
findings.source: Repo B-2379 (FQ2 2010 call p.2708) for the WTO finding; the amounts are model knowledge (WTO panel report WT/DS316/R, 2010), not verified because www.wto.org did not resolve
findings.quote: finding every instance of launch aid challenged by the U.S. to be illegal and harmful to U.S. interests
findings.use_in_model: Airbus's NGSA can expect state loans covering 20-33% of its development, which widens the cost-of-capital gap between the rivals. A Boeing exit would leave narrowbodies to a subsidised rival, which feeds the DC and brand pressure on Boeing.

findings.topic: Airbus is about a quarter state-owned and uses refundable advances
findings.claim: At 31 December 2025 the French state held 10.83% of Airbus (via Sogepa), the German state 10.82% (via GZBV) and the Spanish state 4.08%, about 25.7% in total. Airbus funds development partly through 'European governments' refundable advances' and leads EU Clean Aviation projects. From model knowledge, Airbus was founded in 1970 as a Franco-German consortium.
findings.source: Airbus Board Report FY2025 p.110 (A-0381), p.88 (A-0348), p.157 (A-0445), in /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/airbus/evidence.jsonl
findings.quote: the French State held 10.83% of the outstanding Company shares through Sogepa, the German State held 10.82% through GZBV
findings.use_in_model: Under Do Nothing, the narrowbody market passes to a firm about one quarter owned by European states, whose governments fund its launches. This is the factual basis for the DC 'leaving the market to foreign champions' pressure, though France and Germany are allies, not adversaries.

findings.topic: Boeing's own pledge: future support only on market terms
findings.claim: In July 2021 Boeing welcomed the US-EU understanding that all future government support for developing or producing commercial aircraft must be on market terms, and pledged to back its enforcement. In 2025 Airbus secured a permanent zero-for-zero EU-US aircraft tariff accord.
findings.source: Repo B-1825 / BX-0291 (FQ2 2021 Earnings Call, 28 Jul 2021, p.683); Airbus Board Report FY2025 p.73 (A-0322)
findings.quote: all future government support for the development or production of commercial aircraft must be provided on market terms. We will fully support the U.S. government's efforts to enforce this agreement.
findings.use_in_model: This sharply limits an explicit federal launch subsidy for the fps. A non-market subsidy would contradict Boeing's own stated position and risk the zero-tariff regime. Model the federal share as indirect only (R&D contracts, tax, export credit, siting).

findings.topic: WTO findings on US support to Boeing
findings.claim: From model knowledge: the WTO Appellate Body (March 2012, DS353) found that NASA and DoD R&D contracts, Washington State and Wichita tax breaks and FSC/ETI tax benefits subsidised Boeing's commercial aircraft. The EU put the total at about $5.3B or more for 1989-2006, roughly $0.3B a year, with NASA and DoD R&D about $2.6B of it. That is far below the roughly $18-22B of Airbus launch aid the US alleged.
findings.source: Model knowledge (WTO DS353 reports, 2011-2012; EU and USTR statements), not verified because www.wto.org did not resolve
findings.use_in_model: Historically the federal bill cut on Boeing commercial programmes was a few hundred million dollars a year spread over all programmes, a low single-digit percentage of development. Do not assume more than that without a new policy.

findings.topic: 2020 crisis: Boeing kept the federal option open but used the markets
findings.claim: In April 2020 Boeing welcomed the CARES Act, cited 2.5 million US aerospace jobs and 17,000 suppliers, and listed Treasury and Fed funding as options. It then drew a $13.8B term loan and raised $25B of bonds. From model knowledge, it said it would not seek the CARES Act's $17B for national-security businesses. It still received indirect help: a $1.175B CARES tax benefit from carrying 2020 losses back to 35% years, and faster DoD progress payments.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcripts from 2006-2025_Compressed.pdf p.856 (FQ1 2020 call, 29 Apr 2020; repo B-1668); B-1714 (p.828), B-1722 (p.802); Boeing 10-K FY2020 p.1426 (tax), p.1409 (DoD payments); the $17B and Boeing's decision not to apply are model knowledge
findings.quote: we believe that government support will be critical to ensuring our industry's access to liquidity. We continue to evaluate options in the capital markets as well as funding options from the U.S. government
findings.number: 25 bonds; 13.8 term loan; 1.175 CARES tax benefit; 17 national-security loan pool (memory)
findings.use_in_model: When markets are open, Boeing takes state help in indirect forms (tax, payment terms) and avoids state money that comes with equity or strings. A fps bill cut is therefore more likely to be tax and contract based than direct federal funding.

findings.topic: 2024: Boeing again chose private equity over the state
findings.claim: At Baa3, the edge of junk, Boeing raised about $24B in October 2024 ($18.2B of common stock and $5.7B of mandatory convertible preferred) to defend its investment-grade rating. It did not turn to government support.
findings.quote: the issuance of common stock and Mandatory convertible preferred stock in the fourth quarter of 2024, which resulted in cash proceeds of $18.2 billion and $5.7 billion
findings.use_in_model: Counter-evidence: even under severe stress, Boeing funded itself privately. Do not assume it would accept a state equity stake to fund an fps.

findings.topic: Lockheed L-1011 (1971): rescued, then allowed to exit
findings.claim: In 1971 Lockheed needed a $250M federal loan guarantee to survive the TriStar. From model knowledge, the Emergency Loan Guarantee Act passed the Senate 49-48, and the UK nationalised Rolls-Royce the same year to save the RB211 engine. Lockheed sold about 250 of the roughly 500 TriStars it needed to break even, lost about $2.5B, announced its exit from airliners in December 1981, and never returned. Washington did not try to keep it in the market.
findings.source: franchise_research.json, L-1011 findings, citing GAO PSAD-78-66 https://www.gao.gov/assets/./psad-78-66.pdf and https://aussieairliners.org/l-1011/tristar.html; the Senate vote and the RR nationalisation are model knowledge
findings.use_in_model: The US pays to stop a collapse, not to keep a firm in a market. A precedent for exit without punishment, though Lockheed was the third US maker, not the last.

findings.topic: SST (1971): the only direct federal launch of a Boeing airliner was cancelled
findings.claim: From model knowledge: the federal government funded most of the development cost of the Boeing 2707 supersonic transport (about 75-90%). In March 1971 Congress voted to end funding after about $1B had been spent. Boeing's Seattle employment fell from about 100,800 (1968) to about 38,700 (1971), the 'Boeing Bust'. Washington accepted the job losses and the loss of a prestige programme on cost grounds.
findings.source: Model knowledge, not verified this session (web search budget used up)
findings.use_in_model: Counter-evidence to 'DC will not let Boeing shed jobs': DC once cut more than 60,000 Boeing jobs' worth of programme funding. A prestige or technology argument did not outweigh cost.

findings.topic: Auto rescues: the scale the US will absorb for jobs
findings.claim: From model knowledge: Chrysler received $1.5B of federal loan guarantees in 1979-80 and repaid early, and the Treasury profited on its warrants. GM received about $49.5B under TARP in 2009, and the Treasury exited in December 2013 with a loss of about $11.2B. Both were rescues from insolvency, not funding for new products.
findings.source: Model knowledge (Chrysler Corporation Loan Guarantee Act 1979; US Treasury TARP reports), not verified this session
findings.use_in_model: Shows the US will absorb a loss of more than $10B to save a jobs-heavy national manufacturer in a crisis. It supports a 'Boeing is too big to fail' floor on downside scenarios, not a subsidy for launching the fps.

findings.topic: CHIPS Act: the US template for co-funding strategic manufacturing
findings.claim: From model knowledge: the 2022 CHIPS Act provided about $39B of manufacturing grants plus a 25% investment tax credit. Commerce sized awards at roughly 5-15% of project capital cost, for example $7.86B to Intel in November 2024. It covers semiconductors, not aircraft.
findings.source: Model knowledge (CHIPS and Science Act 2022; Commerce award notices), not verified this session
findings.use_in_model: If Washington framed narrowbody production as strategic manufacturing, a CHIPS-like grant of about 10% of plant capex (not of total development) would be the template. New legislation would be needed, and Boeing's 2021 'market terms' pledge cuts against it.

findings.topic: 2025 US equity stakes and golden shares in strategic firms
findings.claim: From model knowledge, not verified, all 2025 events: the US converted CHIPS grants into about a 9.9% stake in Intel (about $8.9B, August 2025). It took a 'golden share' in US Steel as a condition of Nippon Steel's takeover (June 2025). The DoD bought $400M of MP Materials preferred stock (about 15%) with a 10-year NdPr price floor of about $110/kg (July 2025). The 2026 Boeing calls show no comparable stake in Boeing.
findings.source: Model knowledge, unverified (web search budget used up); I checked /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcript Digest (4).pdf (Boeing 2026 calls) and found no mention of a government stake
findings.use_in_model: A new US willingness to co-fund strategic firms in exchange for equity and control strings. Boeing has avoided this route (2020, 2024). If used, model it as a cost-of-capital benefit offset by governance constraints, for example a block on exiting.

findings.topic: 2025-26: the White House as Boeing's sales agent
findings.claim: Boeing says US trade deals delivered large orders: Qatar (120 787s and 30 777-9s), British Airways and Korean Air. In May 2026 it gained a 200-aircraft Chinese commitment during a presidential visit, reopening China to Boeing narrowbodies after almost ten years without an order. By September 2026 the commitment was still being converted into airline orders.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcripts from 2006-2025_Compressed.pdf p.24 (Morgan Stanley conference, 11 Sep 2025; repo B-2333); /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcript Digest (4).pdf p.84 (FQ1 2026 call, 22 Apr 2026), p.54 (Bernstein conference, 27 May 2026), p.27 (Morgan Stanley conference, 16 Sep 2026); repo B-2321 (orders)
findings.quote: There's no better way to correct the balance of trade than to buy a large number of aircraft. And certainly, we're the beneficiary of that. The administration has been very helpful. / President Trump has been very focused on supporting us in international campaigns
findings.use_in_model: Government support for Boeing comes mainly as demand, not cash. It can raise the fps's share and volume assumptions in politically allocated markets such as China and the Gulf, but it equally props up the MAX in Do Nothing. Value it as a modest volume uplift for a US-built product, and note that it depends on the administration in office.

findings.topic: Ex-Im Bank: DC did not deliver for Boeing for four years
findings.claim: Boeing lobbied 'forcefully' for the Export-Import Bank. Its charter still lapsed on 30 June 2015, until December 2015, and the bank then lacked a board quorum and could not approve large deals until 2019. In 2008, 80% of Boeing's internationally financed deliveries had used Ex-Im; by 2015 about 15% of customers used it as backstop financing.
findings.source: Boeing 10-K FY2017 p.172 and p.185; repo B-1077 (FQ2 2015 call p.1757), B-0088 (FQ1 2008 call p.2934)
findings.quote: We have about 15% of our customers that use Ex-Im financing as backstop financing ... that's why we're so forceful on this topic that it's important Ex-Im be reauthorized.
findings.use_in_model: Counter-evidence: Boeing's weight in DC did not secure even a low-cost policy for about four years. Haircut any assumed federal support for the fps for political reliability.

findings.topic: Brazil and Embraer: state finance and tariff diplomacy
findings.claim: Embraer's 2020 liquidity came partly from Brazil's state bank BNDES and US EXIM, more than $1B in total. In 2025 aircraft were left out of the US 50% tariff on Brazil, after Embraer showed both governments its US jobs and supplier spending; a 10% tariff still applied. Boeing's deal to buy 80% of Embraer's commercial business for $4.2B was terminated by Boeing in 2020. From model knowledge, Brazil's golden share had approved that deal in January 2019, and Brazil became a US Major Non-NATO Ally in 2019.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Embraer Transcripts 2010-2020 (1).pdf p.420 (FQ4 2020 call, 19 Mar 2021) and p.90-91 (FQ2 2025 call, 5 Aug 2025); Boeing 10-K FY2023 p.404 / FY2020 p.1470; golden share and MNNA status are model knowledge
findings.quote: securing more than $1 billion in finance from different sources, such as BNDES, U.S. EXIM ... / We showed them how we contribute to Brazil and how risky it is for us to be subject to a 50% tariff.
findings.use_in_model: Brazil backs Embraer with finance and diplomacy, and the US exempted aircraft even while imposing tariffs on Brazil. The facts do not support calling Brazil a 'declared enemy'. An Embraer route to the fps stays politically feasible, and Brazil could co-finance its share of the work.

findings.topic: WTO Brazil-Canada regional jet subsidy war
findings.claim: From model knowledge: in the Embraer-Bombardier disputes, the WTO authorised Canada to retaliate up to about C$344M a year against Brazil's Proex export-finance subsidies (2000), and Brazil about US$248M a year against Canada (2003). Both states had subsidised their regional jet champions.
findings.source: Model knowledge (WTO DS46 and DS222), not verified because www.wto.org did not resolve
findings.use_in_model: Brazil's and Canada's support has mostly been export finance and interest subsidies, and it drew WTO retaliation on the same scale as the subsidy. This supports a retaliation offset on any state support in the model.

findings.topic: China: state carries the whole COMAC bill
findings.claim: CSIS counted RMB 328.5B (about $49B) of identified state support to COMAC through 2016, and up to $72.1B if continued to 2020, excluding R&D grants, land and tax support. The C919's announced RMB 58B budget was estimated to have ended above RMB 125B (about $20B), so state support exceeds the programme's whole development cost.
findings.source: franchise_research.json COMAC findings, citing CSIS 'China's COMAC: An Aerospace Minor Leaguer', Dec 2020, https://www.csis.org/blogs/trustee-china-hand/chinas-comac-aerospace-minor-leaguer; Boeing 10-K FY2024 p.2167 (repo B-2269) names 'entrants from China' as its only rivals besides Airbus
findings.quote: We face aggressive international competitors who are intent on increasing their market share, such as Airbus and entrants from China.
findings.use_in_model: Under Do Nothing, Boeing's exit leaves room for a rival with no payback constraint, owned by a state the US officially calls its 'pacing challenge'. This is the strongest factual basis for DC pressure against a Boeing exit. Treat it as a political cost of Do Nothing within H8, not as cash.

findings.topic: Japan: METI support did not create a champion, and the exit was allowed
findings.claim: From model knowledge, the Japanese government (METI/NEDO) subsidised about a third of the MRJ's initial roughly ¥150B budget (about ¥50B). Mitsubishi Heavy Industries spent about ¥1 trillion (about $7.6B) and ended the SpaceJet on 7 February 2023 with no deliveries. Tokyo did not stop the exit.
findings.source: franchise_research.json SpaceJet finding, citing MHI notice 7 Feb 2023 https://mhi.com/notice/notice_230207.html; the METI share is model knowledge, not verified
findings.use_in_model: A government's early share was small next to the eventual bill (about 5% of the final cost) and did not prevent exit. State money does not guarantee a viable programme.

findings.topic: UK and Rolls-Royce: a government carrying part of a champion's R&D and its liquidity
findings.claim: Third parties, mainly the UK government, funded about £400M of Rolls-Royce's roughly £1.4B gross R&D a year (about 29%). In 2020, UK Export Finance (UKEF) part-guaranteed a new £2B term loan and indicated support for a further £1B. A later £1B facility was 80% UKEF-guaranteed. Rolls-Royce cancelled the last UKEF-backed loan in 2025, once it was back at investment grade.
findings.source: Repo R-0678 (RR FY2017 call, 7 Mar 2018, p.617); /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcript Digest 2010-26.pdf p.350 (FH1 2020 call, 27 Aug 2020), p.335 (special call, 1 Oct 2020), p.154 (FY2022 call, 23 Feb 2023), p.31 (FY2024 results)
findings.quote: We started for around GBP 1.4 billion, and then we have contributions from third parties of around GBP 400 million. And the U.K. is the significant contributor
findings.use_in_model: A G7 government routinely carries a quarter to a third of a national aerospace champion's R&D and backstops it in crisis. This is the ceiling of what a US 'bill cut' via NASA, DoD or the DoE could aim at for fps technology, not for the airframe programme.

findings.topic: Rolls-Royce left narrowbody engines in 2012 with no political block
findings.claim: Rolls-Royce could not make a business case for an A320neo engine. In 2012 it sold its 32.5% IAE stake for $1.5B and a flying-hours royalty that ends in 2027, cutting about £4B from its order book. I found no record in the repo of UK political pressure against the exit. By 2023 it said it was well placed to 're-enter' narrowbodies with a partner.
findings.source: Repo R-0313, R-0916, R-0919 (FY2011 calls, 9 Feb 2012), R-0468, R-0476 (FY2012 fixed-income call p.1134), R-0812 (FY2020 call p.311); /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Transcript Digest 2010-26.pdf p.91 (Capital Markets Day, 28 Nov 2023)
findings.quote: we could not make a business case to launch a new engine for the NEO ... we've all felt that the best way forward was for us to move out of the partnership at this time. Take in the $1.5 billion.
findings.number: 1.5 proceeds; 32.5 stake; ~4 order book cut; royalty end 2027
findings.use_in_model: Counter-evidence: a state-backed national champion left the narrowbody market on numbers alone, without political or brand punishment. Fourteen years later it is still trying to return with a partner, which shows the long-run cost of exit.

findings.topic: Government 'bill cuts' come back as royalties and job commitments
findings.claim: Canadian federal and provincial agencies reimbursed part of Pratt & Whitney Canada's engineering and development spending in exchange for job commitments and long-term royalties. Pratt converted about 20 years of variable royalties into a fixed settlement, an $867M charge in 2015, paid at about $250M a year in 2016-19.
findings.source: Repo P-1124 (UTC FQ4 2015 call, 27 Jan 2016, p.1802), P-0178, P-0288 (Goldman conference, 14 Nov 2017, p.1365); /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/Filings.pdf p.742 and p.756 (UTC 10-K)
findings.quote: they would provide reimbursement for a portion of our E&D. We had, in turn, promised certain jobs in Canada... we had 20-years-plus of variable, high-royalty payments looking ahead
findings.number: 867 charge; ~250 per year 2016-2019; 20+ years of royalties
findings.use_in_model: Net the value of any state support for the fps against its repayment, royalty and job-commitment terms. The headline cut overstates the economic cut, and job commitments also make a later exit costly.

findings.topic: McDonnell Douglas 1997: Washington accepted the exit of the second US airframer
findings.claim: The FTC cleared Boeing's $13.3B purchase of McDonnell Douglas because Douglas was 'no longer a meaningful competitive force'. Its share of new orders had fallen to 3-4% by 1996. The European Commission made Boeing give up its 20-year exclusive deals. Boeing took a $1.4B charge and ended the MD-80/90 and MD-11. There was no US rescue of Douglas. From model knowledge, the Clinton administration backed the merger against the EC's threat to block it.
findings.source: franchise_research.json McDonnell Douglas findings, citing the FTC statement of 1 Jul 1997 (https://www.ftc.gov/node/51578), EC decision IV/M.877 (https://ec.europa.eu/competition/mergers/cases/decisions/m877_19970730_600_fr.pdf) and the Boeing release of 21 Jan 1998; US political backing is model knowledge
findings.quote: no longer a meaningful competitive force
findings.use_in_model: Washington let a US maker leave airliners when a US champion remained. My inference: under Do Nothing no US airliner maker would remain, so the political cost of Boeing's exit is larger than any precedent. That is a qualitative argument for using the H8 doctrine premium.

findings.topic: Governments usually let smaller champions exit
findings.claim: After Daimler-Benz ended support, Fokker went bankrupt on 15 March 1996 with 5,664 jobs lost, and DASA took a DM2.3B charge; the Dutch state did not rescue it. Saab (1997), BAE regional jets (2001), Fairchild Dornier (2002), Bombardier (2020) and Mitsubishi (2023) also left without being forced back. No airframer that fully left large commercial aircraft has returned. Installed-base support kept its value and was sold or kept.
findings.source: franchise_research.json Fokker finding (FlightGlobal https://flightglobal.com/a-brief-history-of-fokker/9972.article; Deseret News 15 Mar 1996) and its 'base rates for exits' synthesis (inference from cited findings)
findings.use_in_model: Base rate: political pressure did not stop exits by sub-scale players. Caveat (inference): none of them was one half of a duopoly with a 40% share and hundreds of thousands of supplier jobs, so the base rate understates the pressure on Boeing.

findings.topic: Synthesis (own inference): size of a realistic US bill cut for the fps
findings.claim: From the record above, a realistic US bill cut for the fps is about $1-3B of present value at 10.5%. That is a state siting package (about $1.3-2B PV, as in Washington 2003 and 2013), plus federal R&D and tax help (low hundreds of millions), plus demand diplomacy (which moves volume, not cost). That is about 2-5% of a $60-65B programme, far below Airbus-style loans (20-33%), Quebec (about 17%) or COMAC (above 100%). The 2021 'market terms' pledge and WTO retaliation history make an Airbus-style cut unlikely, and it would invite matching support for Airbus.
findings.source: Own inference from the findings above; PVs calculated from evenly spread nominal amounts (WA 2003: $3.2B over 2005-24 gives $1.32B; WA 2013: $8.7B over 2024-40 gives $1.47B in 2013; a $0.3B-a-year package over 2035-54 gives $1.66B in 2030, all at 10.5%)
findings.use_in_model: Enter as a separate, evidenced component of the H8 doctrine premium, capped at $2B: about $1.5B of siting incentives, less a retaliation haircut of about 25%. It closes part of the roughly $4B gap at 10.5% but does not pass the $1B business-case test by itself. It can decide the $1B tie rule, and at 8.1% it strengthens an fps that already beats Do Nothing.

research.summary:
What the evidence shows. When the money was small or the government was the customer, political and strategic pressure has changed Boeing's decisions, and the cost can be measured. When the question was a new airplane or a large commitment, it has not.

Pressure that changed decisions:
- VC-25B (Air Force One): about $2.8B of losses on a roughly $4B fixed-price deal struck under presidential pressure.
- KC-46 tanker: about $9.1B of pre-tax reach-forward losses (2014-2024). Ortberg said in 2024 Boeing "can't walk away" from these contracts.
- T-X and MQ-25: $691M of pre-tax charges taken up front, by choice, in 2018.
- 737 workforce: about $5B of abnormal costs (2020-21) to keep workers and the line through the production suspension.

Pressure that did not:
- Boeing walked away from the NMA, a 4,000-5,000-aircraft segment.
- It ended the Embraer joint venture with Brazil and settled the arbitration for $150M.
- It cut 26,000 jobs in 2020 and moved 787 assembly out of Washington state.
- It turned down CARES Act aid (from memory) and raised $25B of bonds instead.
- It leaves China out of its guidance.
- In May 2026 its leaders said they now turn down risky fixed-price work.

Boeing's own statements say "we will" do a new airplane (Malave, March 2026), but always on three conditions: the market, the technology and Boeing must all be ready.

How the game already handles it. I rebuilt thresholds.decide() on franchise.json; it matches all 1,560 stored decisions. Then I added a strategic premium S to every column of every fps plan and found the smallest S that flips the decision.

| Round | S needed (base, full view, 10.5%), PV 2026 | Same S in that year's dollars |
|---|---|---|
| 2030 | $6.1B | $9.1B |
| 2035 | $4.5B | $11B |
| 2045 | $3.3B | $22B |
| 2050 | $2.5B | $27B |

- The H8 "premium" reading needs the same S as the plain rule. H8 only widens the CEO's choice; the Board's business-case test (beat Do Nothing by more than $1B) and the Re-engine alternative still bind. As coded, the $2B doctrine premium can never rescue an fps that is behind.
- At 8.1%, the 2030 decision flips at S = $1.4B ($1.9B in 2030 dollars). That is inside H8's $2B and inside the premiums Boeing has revealed. So whether 10.5% is a real or a nominal rate decides more than politics does.

Ranking the five options:

1. **(a) A strategic premium S: best supported.** It matches expanded NPV in the literature (Trigeorgis, Myers) and Boeing's own franchise-based bids. Rules:
   - Cap S by premiums Boeing chose up front: about $0.7-5B in the dollars of the decision year (central about $2B, the size of H8).
   - Fill it only with items the franchise terms C1-C6 leave out: political capital in defence and exports, 737-based military aircraft (P-8, E-7), and engineering talent and brand beyond stranded overhead.
   - Apply it to the Board's tests, not only to the CEO's pick.
   - Weaknesses: the size is subjective, and its history is poor. The 2011-2018 strategic bids preceded about $12B of losses, and current leadership has disowned them.
2. **(d) "Never exit the core"**: Boeing says this, but has never been tested on its core. Its record of leaving non-core segments argues against using it as a general rule. Use it only as a backstop at the last round that still avoids a gap (2050), at a known cost of about $1.4B PV 2026 ($15B in 2050 dollars).
3. **(b) Government co-funding**: in 2030 it needs about 26% of the bill (about $17B). That is far beyond US precedent, and trade rules (WTO rulings, the 2021 US-EU "market terms" agreement) limit it. Money from today's administration tends to come with equity strings, which Boeing refused in 2020.
4. **(c) A political cost of exit**: weak. No precedent: Lockheed left airliners in 1981 and was not punished. The defence profits at risk are small: Boeing's defence unit (BDS) has had negative margins since 2022 and made 3.1% in Q1 2026. And a cost dated 2045-60 is heavily discounted.
5. **(e) A lower hurdle rate for strategic programmes**: survey practice runs the other way (firms set hurdles above their cost of capital). It is also untargeted: it lifts the Re-engine too.

Framing check:
- China is officially a US "pacing challenge" or "strategic competitor", not a declared enemy. Brazil has been a Major Non-NATO Ally since 2019, though the US put tariffs on it in 2025.
- In this game the share Boeing gives up goes to Airbus and an unnamed entrant. COMAC is held to its capacity, 3,850 deliveries in 2045-60, whatever Boeing does.

Limits: my WebSearch budget was used up, and faculty.fuqua.duke.edu and www.nber.org are not reachable. Literature figures and 2025 events marked "memory" were not checked in this run.

findings.topic: Game mechanics: the H8 doctrine premium cannot flip the fps
findings.claim: I rebuilt thresholds.decide() on franchise.json's base-point values; it matches all 1,560 stored picks and readings. Adding S to every column of every fps plan, the 'premium' reading (H8, $2B) needs the same S as the 'rule' reading in every 10.5% view. The CEO may give up $2B against the best plan, but the Board still requires an fps item worth more than +$1B against Do Nothing (or the Re-engine), and the Re-engine alone ($3.30B in 2030) sets the bar for the CEO's pick.
findings.source: Own calculation: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-aero-engine-gameboard/95fa875c-ca9d-5564-a6e5-4c9b461d7e56/scratchpad/geo/decision/scripts/s_flip.py on /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/reports/dash-2050-phaseout/data/franchise.json; logic from /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/reports/dash-2050-phaseout/thresholds.py decide() lines 172-216
findings.unit: $B PV 2026: S needed to launch an fps in 2030 / 2035 / 2045 / 2050 (base, full view, 10.5%), the same under the rule and premium readings
findings.direction: toward Do Nothing at 10.5%; shows the existing premium mechanism is inert
findings.use_in_model: Any subjective premium must enter the Board's item tests (business case and downside), not only the CEO's pick, or it never fires. Log S next to H8 and state that H8 alone cannot rescue an fps that is behind Do Nothing.

findings.topic: Game mechanics: S in decision-year dollars rises with delay
findings.claim: Turned into the dollars of each decision year (constant 2026 dollars compounded at 10.5%), the S that flips the decision rises from $9.1B (2030) to $11.2B (2035), $21.7B (2045) and $27.2B (2050). Waiting lowers S in PV-2026 terms only because of discounting; in the money the Board would have to say it is giving up, a late rescue costs more.
findings.source: Own calculation, s_flip.py (second block) on franchise.json, base|full|10.5%
findings.unit: $B in each decision year's constant 2026 dollars (2030 / 2035 / 2045 / 2050)
findings.direction: toward launching early if any premium is to be paid at all; toward Do Nothing otherwise
findings.use_in_model: Compare revealed premiums to S in decision-year dollars, not PV-2026. If a strategic premium is adopted, it is cheapest to honour in 2030.

findings.topic: Game mechanics: at 8.1% a premium inside H8 flips 2030
findings.claim: At 8.1% (10.5% read as nominal), base full view, the 2030 decision flips to the 10-year fps at new sites with S = $1.38B PV-2026 (about $1.9B in 2030 dollars): inside H8's $2B cap and inside the premiums Boeing has revealed. At 8.1% the later rounds need $2.75-4.65B (2035), $4.1-5.2B (2045) and $3.44B (2050) PV-2026, depending on the reading. High-case franchise terms at 8.1% launch in 2030 and 2035 with S = 0.
findings.source: Own calculation, s_flip.py on franchise.json views base|full|8.1% and high|full|8.1%
findings.direction: toward launching the fps, if the rate is read as nominal
findings.use_in_model: Settle whether 10.5% is real or nominal before arguing about politics: the units decide more than any evidence-supported premium. Report the S-to-flip table at both rates.

findings.topic: Game mechanics: cost of a lexicographic 'never exit' rule
findings.claim: Forcing the best fps plan costs, against the plan the CEO would otherwise pick: about $5.1B PV-2026 in 2030 (fps plus Re-engine against the Re-engine alone; about $7.6B in 2030 dollars), $3.3B in 2035, $2.1B in 2045 and $1.4B in 2050 against Do Nothing (about $8B, $14B and $15B in those years' dollars). Low case: $3.5-6.9B PV. High case: $0.5-2.7B PV.
findings.source: Own calculation, s_flip.py on franchise.json (base, low and high full views, 10.5%); Re-engine below the CEO's $1B lever in 2035-50, so Do Nothing is the comparison
findings.direction: neutral: puts a price on rule (d)
findings.use_in_model: If rule (d) is adopted, apply it as a timing constraint at the last round that avoids a product gap (2050 here), and log its known cost as the profile does for H1 ('H1 premium: $2.3B').

findings.topic: Game mechanics: government co-funding needed as a bill cut
findings.claim: Under the base full view at 10.5%, the cut in Boeing's share of the fps bill that launches an fps is 26.0% in 2030 (7-year at Renton; about $17B of the $65B bill), or 19.7% under the premium reading. It is 31.7% in 2035, 62.7% in 2045 and 80.1% in 2050. At 8.1% it is 4.1% in 2030 (10-year, about $2.5B of $60.3B).
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/reports/dash-2050-phaseout/data/franchise.json rounds[n].thresholds[view].rule.cut and .premium.cut; bills from data/thresholds.json (10yr $60.32B, 7yr $65.0B)
findings.direction: toward Do Nothing at 10.5%; toward launching at 8.1% if any support is likely
findings.use_in_model: Option (b): set probability-weighted support p x cut against these thresholds. At 10.5% even p = 1 needs about $17B, beyond any US commercial-aircraft precedent (see the incentives finding). At 8.1%, state-incentive-sized support suffices.

findings.topic: How the profile treats subjective factors now
findings.claim: Government incentives are 'Not modelled; row 13; never in the business case'. Objectives are scored but never change the payoff, and any 'objective premium' shares H8's $2B cap with doctrine premiums. The Board is placed at risk aversion 4.5/5 (downside limit $1B per item, half the CFO's $2B buffer) and time horizon 3/5; pay is 80% financial on 1-3-year metrics.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/profile.md §11.4 row 'Government incentives' (line 468) and H8 (line 31); objectives.md lines 3, 39, 113; board/board.md §4 (risk aversion 4.5, time horizon 3, vote tests table)
findings.quote: Government incentives | ... | Not modelled; row 13; never in the business case
findings.unit: $B H8 cap; risk aversion /5; time horizon /5
findings.direction: toward Do Nothing (the design excludes subjective value by construction)
findings.use_in_model: Any new premium is a design change to H8 and the Board tests. Keep it a separate, logged line that shares the H8 budget, so it is not double counted with the objective premium.

findings.topic: Who gains Boeing's share in this game (China framing check)
findings.claim: In the phase-out world, 2045-60 deliveries are Airbus 18,391, Boeing 4,793, COMAC 3,850 and an unnamed entrant 490. The phase-out moves about 955 Boeing deliveries to Airbus (+465) and the entrant (+490). COMAC is capacity-capped (250 a year from 2050, sold first to its own customers) and gains nothing from Boeing's exit.
findings.source: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/reports/dash-2050-phaseout/data/who_picks_up.json; /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/dashgame/sd_options_phaseout.json third_party
findings.unit: extra COMAC deliveries from the MAX phase-out, 2045-60
findings.direction: toward Do Nothing (weakens the 'leaving the market to China' argument inside this game)
findings.use_in_model: A 'ceding to China' premium has no mechanism in the current world. If geopolitics is to count, add a scenario where COMAC's cap rises or COMAC wins third-country campaigns after Boeing exits; otherwise the premium is about Airbus and an entrant.

findings.topic: Political pressure changed a deal: VC-25B Air Force One
findings.claim: Boeing took a fixed-price deal of about $4B to build two VC-25B presidential aircraft from 747-8s; the 2018 deal followed public presidential pressure on cost (from memory). It then booked reach-forward losses of $168M (2020), $318M (2021), $1,452M (2022), $482M (2023) and $379M (2024). The CEO later said it was a risk Boeing 'probably shouldn't have taken'. In 2025 Ortberg welcomed White House and DOGE involvement in its requirements.
findings.source: Boeing 10-K FY2020 (repo 'Boeing 10ks.pdf' PDF p.1364), FY2023 (PDF p.330, p.382), FY2024 (PDF p.2204, p.2258); BX-0314 (FQ1 2022 call, p.613); BX-1269 (2025-02-20, p.108); BX-1056 (2017-01-25, p.1522). Pre-2018 sequence is from memory, not re-verified
findings.quote: a very unique set ... of risks that Boeing probably shouldn't have taken (Calhoun, BX-0314)
findings.unit: $B pre-tax losses 2020-2024 on a ~$4B programme (sum of five annual charges)
findings.direction: mixed: shows political pressure can buy Boeing's acceptance of a negative-value deal, and that Boeing regrets it
findings.use_in_model: Upper evidence point for a 'political' premium paid under direct White House pressure (about $2.8B, ex post). It was a customer contract, not a commercial launch, so it supports S of a few $B at most.

findings.topic: National-security customer lock-in: KC-46
findings.claim: Boeing bid the KC-46 development phase at zero margin to win what it called a '50-, 60-year widebody franchise'. Pre-tax KC-46 reach-forward losses then summed to about $9.1B: $425M (2014), $835M (2015), $1,128M (2016), $445M (2017), $736M (2018), $148M (2019), $1,320M (2020), $402M (2021), $1,374M (2022), $309M (2023), $2,002M (2024). In 2024 Ortberg ruled out walking away.
findings.source: Repo 'Boeing 10ks.pdf': FY2016 10-K PDF p.1031; FY2019 PDF p.489; FY2020 PDF p.1365; FY2023 PDF p.330 and p.383; FY2024 PDF p.2204 and p.2258. B-0918 (FQ2 2014 call p.1932); BX-1033 (Investor Day 2016 p.1629); B-2203 / BX-1251 (FQ3 2024 call p.148)
findings.quote: I don't think we can walk away from these contracts. These are our core customers that need this capability. (Ortberg, B-2203)
findings.direction: mixed: large persistence, but most of it was unplanned and under contract
findings.use_in_model: Do not use the $9.1B as a revealed ex-ante premium. Ex ante, Boeing chose about zero margin on development; the rest is overrun under a fixed-price contract (and the H5 never-cancel rule). It supports H5 for a launched fps more than a premium to launch one.

findings.topic: Ex-ante strategic premium: T-X and MQ-25 bids
findings.claim: Boeing deliberately took $691M pre-tax ($541M after tax) of charges up front in 2018 to win the T-X and MQ-25 fixed-price competitions. It counted the 'considerable market potential' in the business case, not just the first order, and limited the approach to selected franchises.
findings.source: B-1458 / BX-1151 (FQ3 2018 call, p.1146, Muilenburg); BX-1545 (FQ3 2018 call, p.1150, Greg Smith); BX-1549 (2018-11-07, p.1135); franchise_research.json 'Franchise valuation in Boeing's defense bids'
findings.quote: This strategy reflects a commercial investment mindset, a deliberate and purposeful decision to position ourselves to capture significant future market opportunity (B-1458)
findings.unit: $B pre-tax up-front charge, chosen at bid
findings.direction: toward launching (Boeing does pay explicit strategic premiums), but the size is small
findings.use_in_model: The cleanest revealed ex-ante premium: about $0.7B per franchise bid. Use it as the low anchor for S. The T-7A later lost a further $1.77B in 2024 alone (FY2024 10-K PDF p.2204), so haircut any S for execution risk.

findings.topic: Capability premium: keeping the 737 workforce through the 2020 suspension
findings.claim: Boeing chose to keep its 737 production infrastructure and labour through the 2020 production suspension and low-rate production, expensing about $4B of abnormal costs, later about $5B. It is the largest voluntary payment in the record to keep narrowbody capability.
findings.quote: costs related to our decision to maintain the 737 production infrastructure, including labor during the suspension and low rate production (B-1618)
findings.direction: toward launching (Boeing values narrowbody capability highly)
findings.use_in_model: High anchor for S (about $6B in 2026 dollars). It protected a programme with a huge backlog that would restart, so part of it was ordinary NPV. Do not add it on top of C3 (stranded overhead) in the franchise model, which already prices capacity kept.

findings.topic: Jobs pressure delayed but did not prevent a shutdown (2019-20)
findings.claim: Through 2019 Boeing kept building the grounded MAX at 42 a month, citing '600-some suppliers, hundreds of thousands of jobs', and used $12.4B of cash for inventory. It then suspended 737 production from January 2020.
findings.quote: If you think about our production line against 600-some suppliers, hundreds of thousands of jobs (B-1584)
findings.unit: $B cash used for inventory in 2019 while deliveries were halted
findings.direction: neutral: the jobs argument buys delay, not reversal
findings.use_in_model: Evidence that 'hundreds of thousands of jobs' (Boeing's own phrase, suppliers included) changes timing. Fits a premium that bites at the point of no return (2050 round) rather than an early, unconditional launch.

findings.topic: Workforce and talent weighed in product choices
findings.claim: Boeing's leaders have said that clean-sheet programmes engage the engineering workforce and that Boeing held the only active US airliner design teams. Boeing rebuilt engineering by mass hiring: about 10,000 engineers, and 15,000 hires in 2022 ('we are a technology company'). In 2026 engineering resources roll from the 737-7/-10 and 777X to 'new programs'.
findings.quote: higher risk developments on new airplanes which tend to engage more of the workforce. And we're very mindful of that. (McNerney, B-0444)
findings.unit: hires in 2022, mostly engineers and mechanics
findings.use_in_model: Admissible in S only for talent and brand effects beyond C3 (overhead) and beyond C1's decay terms, e.g. recruiting and certification-base value. Size it small: no Boeing statement prices it.

findings.topic: Boeing's 'we will do a new airplane' doctrine is conditional
findings.claim: Boeing's leaders repeatedly say a successor is inevitable, but always gate it on readiness. Malave (March 2026): 'there will be a day where we have to enter into a new program'. Calhoun (2020): 'We'll do one'. Ortberg (2025): 'we need to be there for the next-generation airplane', with market, technology and Boeing all ready; in October 2026 'nothing has changed'.
findings.quote: it's unrealistic to say that we'll never develop a new program, we will, at the right time. (Malave, digest p.100)
findings.direction: toward launching eventually; neutral on timing
findings.use_in_model: Supports rule (d) only as a backstop: no source shows Boeing treating a 2060 exit as acceptable, but every source keeps the business-case and readiness gates. Encode it as 'launch by the last round that avoids a gap', not 'launch now'.

findings.topic: US government as Boeing's sales agent (2025-26)
findings.claim: Ortberg said Boeing engages the administration daily, 'up to POTUS himself', and that the President 'has been very focused on supporting us in international campaigns'. The China order was '100% dependent on the U.S.-China negotiations'. After the May 2026 presidential trip China committed to about 200 narrowbodies, Boeing's first China narrowbody order in nearly a decade. In 2015 a Xi state visit brought about 300 aircraft.
findings.source: B-2290 (FQ1 2025 call p.76); Transcript Digest (4).pdf p.84 (FQ1 2026 call, 2026-04-22), p.54 (Bernstein conference 2026-05-27), p.27 (2026-09-16); B-1079 (FQ3 2015 call p.1728)
findings.quote: President Trump has been very focused on supporting us in international campaigns, and he's been very successful in doing that. (Ortberg, digest p.84)
findings.unit: aircraft (China narrowbody commitment, May 2026; not yet firm)
findings.direction: toward launching (government support has value only while Boeing has a product to sell)
findings.use_in_model: The political asset is government help in campaigns, already partly in the game's market shares. Count in S only a residual value of being the 'national' supplier that a phase-out would forfeit, and only from the year the exit becomes visible.

findings.topic: Lobbying and regulatory relief are routine tools
findings.claim: Boeing lobbied for Ex-Im reauthorisation (about 15% of customers used it as backstop financing) and won a legislative extension of the MAX 7/10 certification deadline. Under congressional pressure in January 2024 it withdrew its MAX 7 exemption request. It filed a GAO protest within 11 days of losing the 2008 tanker contest, and the protest was sustained.
findings.quote: This is about long-term global competitiveness. And that's why we're so forceful on this topic (Muilenburg on Ex-Im, B-1077)
findings.unit: % of customers using Ex-Im backstop financing (2015)
findings.use_in_model: Government relations are a two-way channel: Boeing gets relief and support and also yields to Congress. Treat it as an asset that depends on Boeing staying a full-line maker (part of S), not as a threat of punishment (option c).

findings.topic: 10-K: dependence on the US government and reputation risk
findings.claim: In 2024, 42% of Boeing's revenues came from US government contracts (including Foreign Military Sales). The government 'may modify, curtail or terminate' contracts at its convenience. Boeing lists reputational harm, US-China trade relations ('remains stalled as economic and national security concerns continue') and ESG expectations ('brand and reputation') as risk factors.
findings.source: Boeing 10-K FY2024, Item 1A risk factors, doc pp.10-14 (repo 'Boeing 10ks.pdf' PDF pp.2176-2180)
findings.quote: In 2024, 42% of our revenues were earned pursuant to U.S. government contracts
findings.unit: % of 2024 revenue from US government contracts
findings.use_in_model: This 42% is the channel for option (c), a political cost of exit. Size any penalty against defence profits (next finding), not revenues.

findings.topic: How much defence profit politics could actually take
findings.claim: BDS had $23.9B of revenue in 2024 with operating margins of -22.6% (2024), -7.1% (2023) and -15.3% (2022). In Q1 2026 its margin was 3.1%; management targets high single digits by the end of the decade. The profit DC could withhold through defence awards is therefore small next to a $60-65B fps decision (inference).
findings.source: Boeing 10-K FY2024 BDS results (repo 'Boeing 10ks.pdf', FY2024 section, MD&A, about PDF p.2203); Transcript Digest (4).pdf p.75 (FQ1 2026) and p.7 (FQ3 2026)
findings.use_in_model: Bound (c): even losing 20% of BDS profit at an 8% target margin is about $0.4B a year (inference). Discounted from 2045-60 at 10.5%, it is a fraction of $1B PV-2026. Option (c) cannot carry the 2030 decision.

findings.topic: Counter-evidence: refusing government money with strings (2020)
findings.claim: In April 2020 Boeing kept government funding open, then raised a $25B bond rather than draw on the CARES Act's $17B set aside for 'businesses critical to maintaining national security' (the CARES detail is from memory). Executives presented the oversubscribed bond as a vote of confidence.
findings.source: B-1668 (FQ1 2020 call p.856); B-1937 (Investor Day 2022 p.416); BX-1636 (FQ2 2020 call p.842); CARES Act s.4003(b)(3) $17B from prior knowledge, not re-verified (WebSearch budget exhausted)
findings.quote: In May, we completed a $25 billion bond issuance (Smith, BX-1636)
findings.unit: $B bond raised vs $B CARES national-security set-aside not used
findings.direction: toward Do Nothing (lowers the chance of option b)
findings.use_in_model: Weight co-funding that carries equity or control conditions with a low acceptance probability. Boeing has preferred markets over state money even in its worst liquidity crisis.

findings.topic: Counter-evidence: job cuts and leaving Washington despite political cost
findings.claim: In 2020 Boeing booked severance for about 26,000 employees. In Q3 2020 it decided to consolidate all 787 production in South Carolina, leaving Everett, Washington, despite the political weight of its home state. It later rehired about 23,000 a year (2022, 2023) when demand returned.
findings.quote: We made the decision during the third quarter of 2020 to consolidate 787 production in South Carolina in 2021, which did not have a significant financial impact on the program. (10-K FY2020)
findings.use_in_model: Job and home-state politics did not stop cost-driven footprint decisions. Do not price jobs as a standalone political cost. Talent value enters only through the narrow admissible part of S.

findings.topic: Counter-evidence: China kept out of the business case
findings.claim: Calhoun removed China from the 2025-26 $10B free-cash-flow target because geopolitical rhetoric 'was beginning to confuse all of our investors'. West built the long-range plan 'ex China'. When China halted deliveries in April 2025 (about 10% of the commercial backlog), Boeing redirected supply and kept its 737 ramp.
findings.quote: I've taken it out of all of our guidance, so our $10 billion in '25, '26 is -- has no China. (Calhoun, B-2052)
findings.use_in_model: Boeing's own practice is to exclude geopolitical upside from business cases. A 'China' premium in S contradicts revealed practice. If used at all, keep it as a scenario column, not a value adder.

findings.topic: Counter-evidence: Embraer and Brazil
findings.claim: In 2018 Boeing called the Embraer deal strategically valuable but not a must-do, and signalled flexibility to 'respect the Brazilian government's priorities'. It terminated the $4.2B (80%) commercial joint venture in April 2020 during its cash crisis. The arbitration ended on 16 September 2024 with Boeing paying $150M under a collar.
findings.source: B-1351 (2018-02-07 p.1311); B-1419 (2018-05-31 p.1226); B-1674 (FQ1 2020 call p.859); B-1792 (10-K FY2020 p.1470); /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/reports/dashboard-fps-delay/review/embraer_analysis_and_check.json (Embraer 20-F FY2024)
findings.quote: I don't see it as a deal that we must do from Boeing's standpoint, but it clearly adds strategic value (Muilenburg, B-1419)
findings.unit: $B deal walked away from / $B arbitration settlement
findings.use_in_model: Boeing's 'strategic value' did not survive a cash crisis, and Brazil's government stance did not hold Boeing in. Discount the 'via Embraer' route and any Brazil-related premium. Brazil is an ally (MNNA), and a Brazil-led narrowbody entrant would not be a US adversary.

findings.topic: Counter-evidence: Boeing cedes segments when the case does not close
findings.claim: Boeing shelved the NMA (a 4,000-5,000-aircraft segment, $15-20B development by Reuters' estimate) in January 2020, ended the 757 (2003-04) and 717 (2005, about $380M of charges), and accepted leaving the 100-150-seat segment to the A220 and Embraer. Its stated test for continuing a programme is forward-looking (remaining revenue over remaining cost).
findings.quote: If it does, we'll go. If not, we've got other investments we can make. (Muilenburg on NMA, B-1586)
findings.unit: aircraft (NMA segment Boeing walked away from)
findings.use_in_model: Limits rule (d) to the core: every exit so far was a non-core segment, and the core 737 franchise has never been tested. Keep (d) out of the default and use it only at the point of no return.

findings.topic: Current leadership has abandoned loss-leader 'franchise' bids
findings.claim: In May 2026 Ortberg said BDS now underwrites new contracts 'with the right baseline' and has 'walked away from some jobs that we historically would have taken on'. The 2011-2018 practice of accepting up-front losses for strategic franchises preceded about $12B of KC-46 and VC-25B losses alone.
findings.source: Transcript Digest (4).pdf p.62 (Bernstein conference 2026-05-27, Ortberg); B-2023 (10-K FY2022 p.1555: $5.25B of 2022 catch-up losses); sums from the KC-46 and VC-25B findings
findings.quote: we've walked away from some jobs that we historically would have taken on ... there's too much risk for the fixed price contract type. So we're not going to do it.
findings.unit: $B KC-46 plus VC-25B losses (2014-2024), my sum
findings.use_in_model: The [NOW] Boeing in the game should apply a smaller, more sceptical S than the McNerney-Muilenburg era. Tag strategic-premium behaviour as [HIST] unless a crisis or a point of no return triggers it.

findings.topic: Government co-funding rarely prevents an exit
findings.claim: Lockheed got a $250M federal loan guarantee in 1971 and still left airliners in 1981. Quebec put in US$1bn for 49.5% of the CSeries (2015), and Airbus took control for a symbolic C$1 in 2017. European governments lent Airbus more than €3.3bn for the A380, which ended in 2019. COMAC has had $49-72bn of identified or potential state support and is still sub-scale.
findings.source: franchise_research.json 'Lockheed L-1011' (GAO PSAD-78-66), 'Bombardier CSeries' (Leeham 2015-10-29, CNBC 2017-10-16), 'Airbus A380' (Airbus FY2018 release; Bloomberg 2019-03-08), 'COMAC C919' (CSIS Dec 2020)
findings.unit: $B state support (Lockheed 1971 / Quebec 2015 / A380 loans, € / COMAC)
findings.use_in_model: Do not treat co-funding as a sure bill cut. Historically it delayed exits rather than reversed weak economics. Weight it as p x cut with p well below 1 and a per-column check.

findings.topic: US precedents for supporting Boeing commercial programmes are small and constrained
findings.claim: Washington State tax incentives (about $3.2B over 20 years for the 787 in 2003; about $8.7B to 2040 for the 777X in 2013, both from memory) were challenged at the WTO, led to 15% EU tariffs on Boeing aircraft, and were repealed. In 2021 Boeing welcomed the US-EU agreement that support for large civil aircraft must be 'on market terms'. NASA's X-66A demonstrator was about $425M of NASA money (memory). All are small against a $60-65B fps.
findings.source: B-1761 (10-K FY2020 p.1369); B-1825 / BX-0291 (FQ2 2021 call p.683); B-0088 and B-1077 (Ex-Im); WA tax figures and NASA X-66A from prior knowledge, not verified in this run
findings.quote: all future government support for the development or production of commercial aircraft must be provided on market terms (Calhoun, B-1825)
findings.direction: toward Do Nothing at 10.5%; neutral at 8.1%
findings.use_in_model: Cap credible co-funding at a few $B of nominal value (about 5-15% of the bill, inference). That is enough only at 8.1%, where a 4.1% bill cut flips 2030. Note that direct launch aid would reopen the WTO dispute that Boeing itself fought.

findings.topic: 2025-26 US state capitalism raises the chance of support, but with strings
findings.claim: In 2025 the US government took about a 10% equity stake in Intel (August, converting CHIPS grants), a DoD equity stake in MP Materials (July), and a 'golden share' in US Steel as a condition of the Nippon Steel deal (June). These show a new willingness to fund strategic firms in exchange for ownership or control.
findings.source: Prior knowledge (training data to mid-2026); not verified in this run because the WebSearch budget was exhausted
findings.unit: % US government equity stake in Intel (Aug 2025)
findings.direction: toward launching (raises p in option b) but with control costs Boeing has refused before
findings.use_in_model: Model option (b) as an equity-for-funding offer, not a grant: a bill cut paired with a dilution or control cost, which the 2020 refusal suggests Boeing values highly. Re-verify these facts before use.

findings.topic: Exiting airliners did not bring political punishment in defence
findings.claim: After leaving commercial airliners (L-1011 production ended 1981-84), Lockheed stayed a leading US defence prime and, as Lockheed Martin, became the largest. McDonnell Douglas declined the MD-XX in 1996 and was absorbed by Boeing with government approval. No precedent shows the US government penalising a domestic firm's defence business for a commercial-airliner exit (inference).
findings.source: franchise_research.json 'Lockheed L-1011: exit and no return', 'McDonnell Douglas: declining the next product'; Lockheed Martin's later defence position from prior knowledge
findings.use_in_model: Base rate for a political penalty on exit is about 0. Note the one break with precedent: Boeing is the only US large-airliner maker, so an exit would leave none. Put that in a low-probability scenario column, not the expected column.

findings.topic: Framing check: China and Brazil
findings.claim: China is officially a 'strategic competitor' (2017 National Security Strategy) and the 'pacing challenge' (2022 National Defense Strategy), not a declared enemy. Brazil has been a US Major Non-NATO Ally since 2019. In July 2025 the US imposed tariffs of up to 50% on Brazil; my recollection is that civil aircraft and parts were exempted. Embraer is exploring a narrowbody with partners (PIF, Korea, Japan, Turkey, India: early stage, unfunded).
