findings.source: Designations and tariff details from prior knowledge (not verified in this run); Embraer partner talks: /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/reports/dashboard-fps-delay/fps_delay_assessment.md
findings.use_in_model: Do not label Brazil an adversary. A 'ceding to adversaries' premium applies, if at all, to COMAC, which the game caps by capacity. A Brazil-led entrant is an allied supplier.

findings.topic: Practice: CFOs use NPV first; few use real options
findings.claim: Graham and Harvey (2001, JFE 60:187-243) surveyed 392 CFOs: about 74.9% always or almost always use NPV and 75.7% IRR, against about 26.6% who incorporate real options. Large firms rely more on NPV and CAPM, and most use a company-wide rather than a project-specific discount rate.
findings.source: Graham, J.R. and Harvey, C.R. (2001), 'The theory and practice of corporate finance: evidence from the field', Journal of Financial Economics 60:187-243. Figures from prior knowledge; faculty.fuqua.duke.edu and www.nber.org were not reachable to re-check
findings.unit: % of CFOs always or almost always using NPV / IRR / real options
findings.direction: toward Do Nothing (supports the Board's NPV-first test)
findings.use_in_model: The Board's business-case test is standard practice. A strategic premium should be a visible adjustment to NPV, as in expanded NPV, not a replacement for the test.

findings.topic: Practice: hurdle rates run above, not below, the cost of capital
findings.claim: Survey evidence finds firms set hurdle rates above their cost of capital: Poterba and Summers (1995) report an average real hurdle of about 12% among Fortune 1000 CEOs, and Jagannathan, Matsa, Meier and Tarhan (2016, JFE) find hurdles several points above WACC, explained by capacity and managerial constraints. I know of no survey showing systematically lower rates for 'strategic' projects (my reading).
findings.source: Poterba and Summers (1995), Sloan Management Review 37(1); Jagannathan et al. (2016), 'Why do firms use high discount rates?', JFE 120(3). From prior knowledge; exact figures not re-verified
findings.use_in_model: Reject option (e) as a 'strategic discount'. It is untargeted: at 8.1% the Re-engine alone also gains ($5.33B against $3.30B in 2030). Keep the 8.1% run only as a units check (real against nominal).

findings.topic: Theory: expanded NPV and real options cut both ways
findings.claim: Myers (1984) and Trigeorgis (1996) define strategic value as growth and flexibility options: expanded NPV = static NPV + option premium. Dixit and Pindyck (1994) show that under irreversibility the option to wait raises the bar for investing now. Dixit (1989) shows that exit and re-entry are hysteretic, so a full exit is hard to reverse.
findings.source: Myers, S. (1984), Interfaces 14(1); Trigeorgis, L. (1996), Real Options, MIT Press; Dixit and Pindyck (1994), Investment under Uncertainty, Princeton; Dixit (1989), JPE 97(3), as summarised in franchise_research.json 'Real-options exit and re-entry (hysteresis)'
findings.quote: hysteresis is significant even when sunk costs are small (Dixit 1989, abstract as rendered)
findings.direction: neutral: supports 'not now' (H1/H2) and 'do not exit for good'
findings.use_in_model: Use expanded NPV as the frame for S, but credit only options not in C1 (continuing value) or the zero re-entry value already assumed. Waiting value supports the falling PV-2026 S, which argues for a point-of-no-return rule (d) over an early unconditional launch.

findings.topic: Theory and evidence on stakeholder objectives and 'license to operate'
findings.claim: Jensen (2001) argues that stakeholder goals without a single value metric leave managers unaccountable ('enlightened value maximisation'). Porter and Kramer (2006) list 'license to operate' as one of four CSR justifications and criticise it as reactive. Bebchuk and Tallarita (2020) find that the 2019 Business Roundtable purpose statement (181 CEOs; I believe Boeing's CEO signed) changed little in practice.
findings.source: Jensen, M. (2001), Journal of Applied Corporate Finance 14(3); Porter and Kramer (2006), HBR Dec; Bebchuk and Tallarita (2020), Cornell Law Review 106. From prior knowledge, not re-verified
findings.direction: neutral: argues for pricing subjective factors explicitly and keeping them small
findings.use_in_model: Put each subjective element in $B with a source and a cap, which is the H8 logging discipline, instead of a qualitative override. The board's own statement that stakeholder and shareholder interests align 'on a long-term basis' (BG-0006) fits this.

findings.topic: Multi-criteria practice: Boeing's three gates are a conjunctive screen
findings.claim: Boeing decides on a new airplane with three gates (market ready, technology ready, Boeing ready), all of which must pass, followed by a two-step authority to offer and authority to launch on a business case. This is a conjunctive or lexicographic multi-criteria screen (Keeney and Raiffa 1976 style), not a weighted score: subjective factors set the gate, NPV picks among passing plans.
findings.source: B-2303 (Bernstein 2025-05-29 p.60); B-2316 (FQ2 2025 p.46); BG-0021 (FQ4 2018 call p.1124); BG-0022 (2019-02-06 p.1101); Keeney and Raiffa (1976), Decisions with Multiple Objectives (prior knowledge)
findings.quote: One is, when is the market ready? And two, when are we ready ... And third is, when is the technology ready? (Ortberg, B-2303)
findings.direction: toward Do Nothing now; neutral later
findings.use_in_model: If politics enters as a criterion, the evidence-consistent form is a gate or tie-breaker (H8's $1B tie rule, or (d) at the point of no return), not a weight that overrides NPV in every round.

findings.topic: Board: long-cycle language, short-cycle pay
findings.claim: The board calls Boeing 'a long-cycle business' whose stakeholder and shareholder interests align over the long term. Calhoun said programmes last 'decades and decades' and that he trusted the board to judge him on that. But long-term pay rests on three-year cumulative free cash flow, and the annual bonus is 80% financial.
findings.source: BG-0006 (2021 Annual Meeting p.754); BG-0010 (FQ1 2022 call p.614); BG-0026 (10-K FY2024 p.2275); /home/user/aero-engine-gameboard/wargame/profiles/boeing/board/board.md §4 (time horizon 3/5)
findings.quote: every one of these programs lasts for decades and decades ... I trust that they will evaluate me on that basis (Calhoun, BG-0010)
findings.unit: years of cumulative FCF in the long-term incentive
findings.direction: toward Do Nothing in 2030; mixed later
findings.use_in_model: The time-horizon score (3/5) limits S: a board paid on three-year cash will not approve a premium of several $B for effects after 2045. A 'national-champion' premium is more credible if the time horizon rises toward 4 once the rating is secure (board.md trend, inference).

design.how_boeing_behaved:
Summary: political, jobs and brand pressure has changed where Boeing builds, on what terms, and how it handles safety and government-customer contracts. It has not yet made Boeing launch, or keep, a commercial programme whose numbers failed. Boeing has never been tested on leaving its core 737 market, and every precedent below is for a smaller exit. That is the gap the subjective premium S has to cover.

WHERE PRESSURE CHANGED THE DECISION, AND WHAT IT COST
- Government-customer contracts.
  - VC-25B (Air Force One): Boeing accepted a fixed-price deal of about $4B under presidential pressure (pre-2018 sequence from memory). It then lost $2.8B in 2020-24 (10-K FY2020 p.1364; FY2023 p.330 and p.382; FY2024 p.2204 and p.2258). Calhoun called these "risks that Boeing probably shouldn't have taken" (BX-0314, p.613).
  - KC-46 tanker: Boeing bid development at about zero margin for a "50-, 60-year widebody franchise" (BX-1033). It then lost about $9.1B in 2014-24 (my sum of 10-K charges). Ortberg said in 2024: "I don't think we can walk away from these contracts" (B-2203, p.148).
  - T-X and MQ-25: Boeing took $691M of charges up front in 2018, by choice (B-1458, p.1146).
- Capability and jobs.
  - In 2019 Boeing kept building the grounded MAX at 42 a month, citing "600-some suppliers, hundreds of thousands of jobs" (B-1584, p.965), and used $12.4B of cash for inventory. It then suspended production in January 2020.
  - It kept the 737 workforce and line through the suspension, at about $5B of abnormal costs (B-1618, p.898; B-1794, p.722).
  - Jobs pressure bought delay, not reversal.
- Safety and certification. Under Senate pressure in January 2024, Boeing withdrew its request for a MAX 7 exemption (B-2140, p.252).
- Terms and site. Boeing turned political pressure into cash:
  - Washington's 2013 777X package: $8.7B nominal, with a site competition among more than 12 states (Transcripts p.2056).
  - South Carolina: $346M of cash grants (10-K FY2024 p.2257), a 2009 package of $450-900M, and $120M of bonds in 2025.
- Trade peace. In 2020 Boeing asked Washington state to repeal its own tax preference to remove the basis of the EU's WTO tariffs (10-K FY2020 p.1369, B-1761; Fortune, 20 Feb 2020). In 2021 it endorsed "market terms" for all future support (B-1825, p.683).
- Selling through Washington. In 2025-26 the administration acted as Boeing's sales agent: Qatar, Korean Air, and the 200-aircraft China commitment of May 2026. Ortberg: "my primary objective was to reopen that market to our narrowbody airplanes" (Transcript Digest (4) p.54 and p.84). This supports existing products; it is not launch money.

WHERE PRESSURE DID NOT CHANGE THE DECISION
- Job cuts: about 10,000 in 2009 (B-0147), 26,000 in 2020 (B-1767) and 17,000 in 2024 (B-2206).
- Moves out of Washington state:
  - 787 second line to North Charleston in 2009 (B-0218). The NLRB complaint was dropped in December 2011 and the siting stood.
  - All 787 production to South Carolina in 2020 (10-K FY2020 p.1375), despite Governor Inslee calling it "an insult".
  - About 300 engineering jobs moving to South Carolina in 2026 (Spokesman-Review, 5 Feb 2026).
- Segment exits:
  - 757 (2004) and 717 (2005).
  - 747, last delivery 31 Jan 2023.
  - 767 freighter ending 2027, with $580M of losses (B-2246).
  - NMA shelved in 2020 (B-1620, p.902).
  - The 100-150 seat segment conceded to the A220 and E2 (B-1666, p.869).
  - The Embraer joint venture terminated on 25 Apr 2020 (B-1674, p.859) and settled for $150M in September 2024.
- Government money with strings refused:
  - CARES Act $17B set-aside not used; $25B of bonds raised instead (B-1668; BX-1636).
  - $24.25B of private equity raised in October 2024 rather than state support (B-2258).
- NASA X-66A demonstrator paused in April 2025 (AIAA, 25 Apr 2025).
- China removed from guidance: "our $10 billion in '25, '26 ... has no China" (B-2052, p.315).
- 2026 brought COMAC's first international route, the ITIF report and the Section 232 finding. Boeing's CFO still said: "That day is not today, and it's not any time near" (Malave, Digest (4) p.100). On 27 Oct 2026 Ortberg said "nothing has changed" (Digest p.16).
- Current leadership has dropped the loss-leader bids: "we've walked away from some jobs that we historically would have taken on" (Digest p.62).
- No US official or member of Congress has asked for a 737 successor (gap in the dc-jobs sweep's searches).

PRECEDENTS FOR EXIT WITHOUT PUNISHMENT
- Lockheed left airliners in 1981 after about $2.5B of L-1011 losses and became the largest US defence prime.
- The FTC cleared the 1997 McDonnell Douglas merger, finding Douglas "no longer a meaningful competitive force".
- Rolls-Royce sold out of IAE in 2012 (R-0313).
- Fokker (1996), Mitsubishi (2023) and Bombardier (2020) also left.
- Caveat (inference): none of these was half of a duopoly. Boeing would leave the US with no airliner maker, so the political stakes exceed every precedent.

WHAT BOEING SAYS ABOUT IDENTITY
- Boeing's leaders say a successor will come, always with conditions:
  - Ortberg: "Boeing's an airplane company ... we need to develop a new airplane" (B-2217).
  - Calhoun: "We'll do one" (B-1620).
  - Malave: "we will, at the right time" (Digest p.100).
- The test is always three gates: market, technology and Boeing ready (B-2303). Muilenburg: "It will not be based on market share" (B-1131).
- Synthesis (inference): the evidence supports a small, capped premium. It does not support an open-ended override. Boeing's revealed doctrine points to a premium that bites at the point of no return rather than early.
design.geopolitics:
CORRECTING THE FRAMING
- China is not a "declared enemy". US strategy documents call it a strategic competitor (2017-18 National Security Strategy and National Defense Strategy language) and the "pacing challenge" (2022 National Defense Strategy). This is from memory: my web-search budget ran out in this step, and any 2025-26 strategy wording was not checked.
- The Pentagon added COMAC to its Section 1260H list of Chinese military companies on 6 Jan 2025 (Aviation Week; Federal Register 2025-00070). That is a security designation of COMAC, not a state of enmity.
- Brazil has been a US Major Non-NATO Ally since 2019 (memory; not re-verified this step). The 2025 US action against Brazil was a national-emergency tariff (EO 14323, 30 Jul 2025) over the Bolsonaro prosecution and court rulings on speech, not a strategic-adversary designation.
  - Even that order exempted civil aircraft and parts. Embraer paid only the 10% baseline tariff, $54M in 2025 (Embraer FQ4 2025 call p.42).
  - The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on 20 Feb 2026. Brazilian aircraft have faced zero US tariff since February 2026 (Holland & Knight, March 2026; Embraer call p.48).

CHINA (keep separate from Brazil)
1. China's weight for Boeing.
   - 21.5% of commercial airplanes (BCA) revenue in 2018; 7.9% in 2020 (10-K FY2018 p.2604; FY2020 p.1471).
   - One 737 in three went to China in 2015-18 (B-1537).
   - About 10% of the commercial backlog in April 2025 (B-2292).
   - Boeing's 2026 China outlook: 7,215 single-aisle deliveries in 2026-45, about 21.5% of world single-aisle demand (Boeing release, 3 Nov 2026; search excerpt).
2. US policy is transactional, not protective.
   - Export licences for COMAC were suspended in May 2025, restored in July 2025, and capped in October 2026 to gain leverage over rare earths (Asia Times citing Reuters, 1 Oct 2026).
   - The May 2026 deal paired China's 200-aircraft commitment with a US pledge of "strict supply guarantees" for aircraft engine parts (China's Commerce Ministry via CNBC, 20 May 2026). Washington traded COMAC's supply security for Boeing orders.
   - The Section 232 proclamation (9 Jul 2026) found that aircraft imports threaten national security but set no tariffs.
3. COMAC is slow but backed by the state.
   - About 13-15 C919 deliveries in 2025 and 11 through September 2026.
   - EASA approval is expected around 2028-31.
   - It depends on the LEAP-1C engine until the Chinese CJ-1000A arrives, around 2030.
   - CSIS counts $49-72B of state support.
4. In this game, COMAC is capped by capacity and gains nothing from Boeing's exit. The MAX phase-out moves about 955 Boeing deliveries in 2045-60 to Airbus (+465) and an unnamed entrant (+490) (data/who_picks_up.json). Airbus already holds about 55% of China's fleet and has a second Tianjin line.
5. Conclusion. "Leaving the market to China" has no cash mechanism in the game. It enters only as:
   - a scenario (G9) in which COMAC is uncapped or exports after EASA approval, which raises the political salience in G5 and the doctrine weight in S;
   - a China market-access sensitivity (G8).
   The base adds nothing, which matches Boeing's own practice of planning ex-China (B-2052).

BRAZIL AND EMBRAER (separate from China)
- Embraer is allied and tied into the US supply base:
  - more than 40% US content; Pratt & Whitney GTF engines on the E2;
  - about 2,500 direct US jobs plus about 10,000 at suppliers (CEO figures);
  - C-390 sales to NATO members, and a Northrop KC-390 tanker team aimed at the USAF (Breaking Defense, Feb 2026).
- Embraer is small next to the 737:
  - 78 commercial deliveries in 2025 and a target of 120 a year by about 2030, against about 564 737s a year at rate 47;
  - 2025 free cash flow of $0.49B;
  - no narrowbody decision before about 2030 (Embraer calls, Feb 2025 to May 2026).
- Embraer said in 2016 it would "look again" if Boeing and Airbus left a segment. Any Embraer-led entrant would bring Saudi, Turkish or Indian partners, not US adversaries.
- The game's "fps via Embraer" variant (Embraer funds 35% of capex) implies $21-23B: about 3 times Embraer's revenue and 45 times its free cash flow. It is not feasible without a backstop from the Brazilian state (BNDES) or a sovereign fund.
- In 2020 Boeing walked away from Embraer despite Brazil's golden-share conditions, and paid only $150M.
- Conclusion: no adversary premium for Brazil. Embraer matters as a constraint on the JV variant (G10), and as the likely identity of the game's allied entrant.

US INDUSTRIAL POLICY, 2025-26
- Washington took equity in strategic firms: Intel 9.9% (August 2025), MP Materials about 15%, and a golden share in US Steel.
- On 26 Aug 2025 Commerce Secretary Lutnick named Boeing among firms where stakes were being discussed (Al Jazeera). No Boeing stake has been reported.
- This makes state launch support with strings (G3) a live scenario. Boeing's 2020 and 2024 refusals of state money argue that it would put a high governance cost on any such offer.

OTHER CONTEXT
- Airbus is about 25.7% owned by the French, German and Spanish states (Airbus FY2025 Board Report p.110, A-0381).
- Airbus builds A320s and A220s in Mobile, Alabama: three lines and more than 2,000 staff.
- So under Do Nothing the share goes mainly to an allied, partly state-owned firm with some US final assembly. It does not go to an adversary.

terms.name: G1 State siting and retention incentives
terms.what_it_captures: Cash from the political weight of jobs. When Boeing launches a programme, states bid for its site. Renton plans get a Washington retention package, like the 777X in 2013. New-sites plans get a competitive auction, like the 787 in 2003 and 2009.
terms.how_it_enters: Premium on fps plans. Added to every column of each fps plan: add_p = I_site(p) x (1 - h) x (1+r)^-(t-2026). I_site is I_renton for the three Renton plans and I_new for the new-sites plans; t is the decision year; h is the haircut in G4. Base PV-2026 at 10.5%: new sites $0.75B in 2030, $0.46B in 2035, $0.17B in 2045, $0.10B in 2050. Renton: $0.50B, $0.31B, $0.11B, $0.07B.
terms.unit: $B in decision-year money (constant 2026 dollars, PV at the decision date), before haircut h
terms.derivation: Washington 2003 package for the 787: $3.2B nominal over 20 years, about $1.3B PV at 10.5% (states sweep; amount from memory). Washington 2013 package for the 777X: $8.7B nominal to 2040, about $1.47B PV in 2013, about $2.1B in 2026 dollars. South Carolina cash grants: $346M (10-K FY2024 p.2257), or $0.49B in 2026 dollars; its 2009 package was $450-900M. Base is about 70% of the Washington precedent, because jobs pledges did not hold and Washington repealed its break in 2020. A new site competes harder than a retention package, so new sites get more.
sources: Transcripts 2006-2025 p.2056 (4 Dec 2013, 777X site competition, 12+ states)
Boeing 10-K FY2024 p.2257 and FY2023 p.382 (South Carolina cash grants $346M)
heraldnet.com: $305M of tax savings in 2015 and $242M in 2016 (search excerpts)
Leeham, 1 Oct 2020 (787 consolidation to South Carolina); Spokesman-Review, 5 Feb 2026
FlightGlobal / Everett Herald, Sept 2024: the IAM 2024 next-airplane clause
terms.evidence_strength: Medium. The precedents are documented in 10-Ks and transcripts; the size for the fps is my inference. The 2024 IAM clause ties a launch before about 2028 to Puget Sound. The game's rounds start in 2030, but a 2028 renewal could remove the new-sites auction.
terms.overlap_with_franchise_terms: None of C0-C6. Count only tax and grant value tied to the programme. Do not also lower the fps bill in thresholds.py (k), and do not count labour concessions already in the game's margins. Jobs pledges are not cash.

terms.name: G2 Federal technology co-funding (NASA, DoD, DoE)
terms.what_it_captures: Federal research money for fps technology, such as a truss-braced wing, engines or thin wings. These are demonstrators, not the airframe programme.
terms.how_it_enters: Premium on fps plans: add_p = G2 x (1 - h) x (1+r)^-(t-2026), in every column. Base PV-2026 at 10.5%: $0.15B in 2030, $0.09B in 2035, $0.03B in 2045, $0.02B in 2050.
terms.derivation: NASA committed $425M to the X-66A against about $725M from Boeing and partners, and the flight programme was paused in 2025. The WTO case DS353 found about $2.6B of NASA and DoD research support for 1989-2006, about $0.15B a year (from memory). The high case assumes two X-66-scale demonstrators.
sources: B-1825 (FQ2 2021 call p.683): Boeing backs 'market terms' support
WTO DS353 Appellate Body, March 2012 (from memory; www.wto.org did not resolve)
terms.evidence_strength: Medium for the precedent; low for the size.
terms.overlap_with_franchise_terms: None. Keep it out of the fps bill and the margin, so it is not counted twice through a technology-driven margin assumption.

terms.name: G3 Federal launch support with strings (scenario only)
terms.what_it_captures: A Washington offer to fund part of the fps in exchange for equity, a golden share or a veto on exit, on the 2025 Intel, MP Materials and US Steel pattern. It is the 'DC will not let Boeing leave' channel.
terms.how_it_enters: Bill cut, in a scenario column. Boeing's share of the bill becomes k = 1 - c in thresholds.values(). Subtract a governance cost gamma x c x bill x df(EIS), and apply the haircut (1 - h). Base probability is 0. Compare c with the stored thresholds in franchise.json for base|full|10.5%, rule reading: 26.0% in 2030 (about $17B of the $65B 7-year bill), 31.7% in 2035, 62.7% in 2045 and 80.1% in 2050. At 8.1% the 2030 threshold is 4.1%.
terms.unit: % of Boeing's fps bill (gamma as a share of its value)
terms.derivation: CHIPS-style grants were 5-15% of project capital cost (Intel received $7.86B, from memory). Airbus's 1992 ceiling was 33%. Quebec carried about 17% of the CSeries. No US precedent exists for a commercial-airliner launch. Boeing refused CARES Act money with equity strings in 2020 and raised $24.25B privately in 2024, so it would put a high governance cost on any such offer.
sources: Gulf News, 30 Apr 2020; B-1668 (FQ1 2020 call p.856); BX-1636
terms.evidence_strength: Low as a probability, medium as a precedent. No official has proposed it.
terms.overlap_with_franchise_terms: None, but it conflicts with G1, G2 and G4. If G3 is used, raise h, because the EU would treat it as launch aid. The governance cost (an exit veto) would make C6 closing costs and H5 permanent.

terms.name: G4 Retaliation and reversal haircut on government support
terms.what_it_captures: The chance that state support for the fps is challenged at the WTO, matched by support for Airbus's NGSA, or repealed.
terms.how_it_enters: A multiplier (1 - h) on G1, G2 and G3.
terms.unit: share of the headline value lost (low/base/high ordered by value to the fps)
terms.derivation: The EU was authorised about $3.99B a year of tariffs over a single Washington tax break. Boeing itself sought the repeal in 2020. The 2021 truce was extended from 11 Jul 2026, but the subsidy dispute is unresolved. Boeing's 2021 'market terms' pledge makes direct support self-contradictory.
sources: Bloomberg, 25 Jun 2026: EU extends its tariff suspension
Fortune, 20 Feb 2020; NW News Network, 12 Mar 2020
terms.evidence_strength: High that the risk exists; the size is inference.

terms.name: G5 Political cost of exit to Washington (probability x amount)
terms.what_it_captures: Lost goodwill in Washington, through defence awards, FAA rate approvals, Ex-Im and trade-deal support, once a narrowbody exit becomes visible. Under Do Nothing that happens from about 2045, when the MAX runs off with no successor.
terms.how_it_enters: Exit cost. Charge -X to Do Nothing and to the Re-engine-only plans in every column; this is mechanically the same as +X on every fps plan. X = p x L x a(20 years, r) x (1+r)^-(t_exit - 2026), with t_exit = 2045 (base). It is a fixed-date cash flow, so it has the same PV-2026 in every round. Base: $0.11B at 10.5%, $0.19B at 8.1%. High: $0.67B and $1.08B.
terms.unit: probability; $B a year of profit at risk
terms.derivation: L is 20-30% of defence (BDS) profit at risk: about $27B of revenue at the 8% target margin, about $2.2B a year (my inference). BDS margins were -22.6% (2024) and 3.1% (Q1 2026). p is low because no precedent shows punishment: Lockheed (1981), Boeing's own 757, 747 and 767F exits, the 2020 job cuts and the 787 move all passed without it, and the F-47 and F/A-XX awards look merit-based. It is not zero because Boeing would be the last US airliner maker, Washington controls the 737 rate cap (38, then 42, then 47), and it switched supplier on Air Force One.
sources: Boeing 10-K FY2024 Item 1A (42% of revenue from US government contracts), PDF p.2177
Transcript Digest (4) p.75 and p.7 (BDS margins, 2026)
CNBC, 17 Oct 2025; Lynnwood Times, 31 May 2026 (FAA rate cap)
FlyingMag / KSL, May 2025 (Air Force One, Qatari 747-8 via L3Harris)
terms.evidence_strength: Low. The channel is real, but there is no measured precedent. The jobs figures (1.5M from Boeing, 1.8M from Commerce) are multiplier estimates, not cash.
terms.overlap_with_franchise_terms: C6 closing costs already carry severance, site closure and supplier termination, so leave every jobs-related cash cost out of L. C4 already prices widebody share lost when Boeing is not full-line, so leave Washington's help on widebody campaigns out of L. Count only defence and Ex-Im goodwill.

terms.name: G6 Military aircraft on the 737 line (P-8, E-7)
terms.what_it_captures: The Defense Department's stake in a live Boeing narrowbody line for surveillance and maritime patrol derivatives after the MAX ends.
terms.how_it_enters: Exit cost on Do Nothing after the MAX line ends (equivalently a premium on fps plans): about $0.15B a year of derivative profit for 10 years after 2060.
terms.derivation: My estimate: 0.15 x a(10 years, 10.5%) x 1.105^-34 = $0.03B. It is negligible as cash. Its importance is as a lobby: Congress restored the E-7 and required $1.1B, and the House backed $1.55B more in June 2026. That lobby raises the probability of G2 and G3, so log it there.
sources: Defense News, 25 Jun 2026 ($1.55B for the E-7)
10-K FY2024 p.2201 (767F ends 2027; KC-46 stays on the 767 line)
terms.evidence_strength: Medium for the lobby; low for the cash.
terms.overlap_with_franchise_terms: C3 is commercial-only (BCA overhead), so there is no overlap. Do not also add defence overhead to C3.

terms.name: G7 Order flow from US trade diplomacy (excluding China)
terms.what_it_captures: Orders won through presidential deals: Qatar, Korean Air, Japan, the UK and Turkey in 2025-26. Commerce counted $215B of 2025 contracts for Boeing and GE.
terms.how_it_enters: Premium on fps plans, through share. Add +x Boeing share points to fps deliveries from entry into service, valued at share_point_pv x (1 - MAX unit profit / fps unit profit). That is 0.634 x (1 - 3.84/14.1) = $0.46B PV-2026 per share point for a 10-year fps launched in 2030 (franchise.json calibration). It scales down for later launches.
terms.unit: Boeing share points of fps deliveries
terms.derivation: Base is zero because both options keep Washington's help while Boeing sells narrowbodies, the game's shares already reflect it, and Axios notes some orders would have come anyway. The high case credits a differential only where a US product exists and the MAX would not.
sources: Reuters via MarketScreener, 23 Jan 2026 ($244B of Commerce-assisted contracts)
Transcript Digest (4) p.84 (Ortberg: 'supporting us in international campaigns')
B-1077 (Ex-Im used as backstop by 15% of customers)
terms.evidence_strength: Medium for the behaviour; low for the differential.
terms.overlap_with_franchise_terms: C1 holds Boeing's share at its last value after 2060, so do not add a share uplift in C1 years as well. C4: do not add a widebody uplift.

terms.name: G8 China market access (US-China political risk)
terms.what_it_captures: China's single-aisle demand (about 21.5% of the world's in 2026-45) and Beijing's habit of allocating orders and stopping deliveries according to the state of relations.
terms.how_it_enters: Sensitivity on Boeing's share in fps years; a delivery-stop shock hits both options while each builds narrowbodies. Base 0, as Boeing values its plans ex-China. Discount politically announced Chinese orders by about 40-50% until they are firm (inference from the 58% Phase One fulfilment rate).
terms.derivation: Shock: about $1B per 50 aircraft for a year (B-2293), but Boeing re-slots China orders to other customers (B-2292; Digest p.65), so the differential cost is small. High: the 2026 reopening holds and adds about 1 share point. Ortberg called the China order '100% dependent on the U.S.-China negotiations'.
sources: PIIE Phase One tracker via SCMP and GTR (search excerpts)

terms.name: G9 COMAC 'ceding to China' scenario (no cash in the base)

Raise COMAC's capacity cap to its own plan (200 a year by about 2032, with exports after EASA approval around 2028-31) and let COMAC take part of the share Boeing gives up. In that scenario raise p in G5 from 0.2 to 0.5 and log the national-security part of S separately. It never adds cash in the base case.

terms.evidence_strength: Low as a trigger; Boeing has never cited COMAC as a reason to launch.
terms.overlap_with_franchise_terms: C4 and the game's share engine. If COMAC is uncapped, C4 and the price terms change through the engine, so do not add a separate share loss.

terms.name: G10 Brazil and Embraer (constraint, no adversary premium)
terms.what_it_captures: Embraer as a possible partner or post-exit entrant, and the feasibility of the 'fps via Embraer' variant.
terms.how_it_enters: Constraint. Cap Embraer's share of the fps capex at 5-10% unless a Brazilian state or sovereign fund co-funds. Treat the unnamed entrant's 490 deliveries in 2045-60 as an allied supplier. Add nothing to Do Nothing for 'ceding to Brazil'.
terms.high: 35% only with a Brazilian state backstop
terms.unit: Embraer's share of the fps capex
terms.derivation: 35% of a $60-65B bill is $21-23B, about 3 times Embraer's 2025 revenue of $7.6B and 45 times its free cash flow of $0.49B. Embraer's own 'go bigger' studies have no decision before 2030. Brazil is a Major Non-NATO Ally (memory), and Embraer has more than 40% US content.
sources: Embraer FQ4 2025 call (6 Mar 2026) p.41-42 and p.48
Embraer FQ3 2016 call p.695 ('we will look again')
EO 14323 via presidency.ucsb.edu; Holland & Knight, Mar 2026
terms.overlap_with_franchise_terms: None. The entrant's share is already in the game's engine.

terms.name: G11 Implicit federal backstop ('too important to fail')
terms.what_it_captures: Washington's readiness to rescue a national champion: the $17B CARES set-aside, the lenient DOJ deal, and the 2025 equity stakes. It could be read as softening the downside and rating tests.
terms.how_it_enters: Constraint, recommended unchanged. Do not relax the -$1B downside test or the -$2B rating buffer.
terms.derivation: Boeing funded itself privately in 2020 ($25B of bonds) and 2024 ($24.25B of equity), at Baa3, and the Board's doctrine puts the rating first (board.md: risk aversion 4.5). A backstop from Washington comes with strings that Boeing refuses (see G3).
terms.evidence_strength: High that Boeing does not rely on it.

terms.name: K1 Brand cost of a failed launch (counter-term)
terms.what_it_captures: The evidence that Boeing's measured brand costs came from failures in execution: the MAX cost about $20B directly and market value fell from about $240B to about $112B. A rushed prestige launch carries a cost-overrun tail; the 787 ran about 5 times its first budget.
terms.how_it_enters: A negative premium on fps plans (sensitivity): -q x overrun x bill x df.
terms.unit: $B PV-2026 for a 2030 launch (low/base/high ordered by value to the fps)
terms.derivation: Base 0, because the game's bill is the planning value and adding the tail would only widen the gap. It is shown so that a brand premium in S is not credited without its downside. Low case: about a 20% chance of a 30% overrun on $60B, discounted.
sources: Repo financials.md section 3 (787 costs); Leeham, 19 Oct 2015
Brand Finance 2026: the brand rose 34% to $24.4B with no new airplane
terms.overlap_with_franchise_terms: The game's fps bill and two-front strain. Do not add it on top of an overrun already in the bill.

terms.name: K2 Lower cost of capital for a more defence-heavy Boeing (counter-term)
terms.what_it_captures: The Lockheed path: after leaving airliners, a defence-heavy firm carries a much lower equity beta (Lockheed about 0.1-0.3, Boeing about 1.2-1.4).
terms.how_it_enters: Rate, on Do Nothing's post-exit years. Sensitivity only; it favours Do Nothing.
terms.unit: $B PV-2026 (low/base/high ordered by value to the fps)
terms.derivation: Speculative: the beta comparison comes from a search excerpt, and a cost-plus F-47 and F/A-XX book supports it. Not sized in the base.
terms.overlap_with_franchise_terms: The 10.5% vs 8.1% rate question. Do not double-count it with a lower rate.

terms.name: S Strategic premium (subjective)
terms.what_it_captures: What the cash-like terms and C0-C6 leave out: standing as the national champion and last US airliner maker, engineering and science identity, the employer brand and talent beyond C3, and the doctrine 'never exit the core'. These are the user's subjective elements.
terms.how_it_enters: Premium on fps plans. V'[p][j] = V[p][j] + S for every fps plan (solo and paired) in every column j. It therefore passes through the CEO's pick, the business-case test (beat the plan without the fps by more than $1B), the downside test (no column below -$1B), the rating test (risk column within $2B of Do Nothing) and the H8 reading. The pair-vs-solo test for a Re-engine beside the fps is unaffected. Solve S_flip per round, view, rate and reading. Then S_residual = S_flip minus the cash-like items G1-G8. Compare S_residual, in decision-year money (x(1+r)^(t-2026)), with the revealed-premium ladder. Cap S at H8's $2B stated in decision-year money, and share that cap with the objective premium. Log every value.
terms.unit: $B in decision-year money (constant 2026 dollars); in PV-2026, divide by (1+r)^(t-2026)
terms.derivation: Base: the clean ex-ante rung, T-X and MQ-25 at $0.91B in 2026 dollars, up to H8's $2B; the 747-8's 2008-09 charges ($3.1B) and the Washington repeal ($1.1-3.2B) sit beside it. High: VC-25B at $3.2B, accepted under presidential pressure but an ex-post loss. Upper bound: the 737 workforce at $6.3B, mostly ordinary NPV. Zero rung: segment exits, the Embraer exit, China upside, and any year when the rating buffer binds. Results (franchise.json base point; my re-implementation of decide() reproduces 4,610 of 4,610 stored decisions): see recommended_method.
sources: Own calculation: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-aero-engine-gameboard/95fa875c-ca9d-5564-a6e5-4c9b461d7e56/scratchpad/geo/design/scripts/design.py and units.py on data/franchise.json
terms.evidence_strength: Subjective by construction. The comparison ladder is evidence-based (high for amounts, medium for comparability).
terms.overlap_with_franchise_terms: Must exclude: C1 (profit after the counted window), C2 (services), C3 (stranded overhead, including engineering overhead), C4 (widebody brand and full-line effect), C6 (closing and severance), the zero re-entry value already given to Do Nothing, every G term, and the 50/50 objective premium, which shares the H8 budget. Talent value is admissible only beyond C3, for example recruiting and spillover to defence.

Scaled by contract value (about 7%), it would be about $4B on a $60B fps bill. The T-7A then lost a further $1.77B in 2024, and current leadership has disowned the approach (Digest (4) p.62).

revealed_premiums.amount: About $5B of abnormal production costs in 2020-21 (about $4B in 2020 and $1B in 2021). That is about $6.3B in 2026 dollars, deflated year by year.

revealed_premiums.amount: $2.8B of reach-forward losses: $168M (2020), $318M (2021), $1,452M (2022), $482M (2023), $379M (2024). That is $3.2B in 2026 dollars, deflated year by year.

revealed_premiums.amount: $9.1B of pre-tax reach-forward losses in 2014-24 (my sum of 10-K charges). That is $11.2B in 2026 dollars, deflated year by year. The ex-ante premium was the forgone development margin and was not sized.

design.recommended_method:
1. Keep the franchise model as built (views game, core, core+overhead, full; base, low and high; 10.5% and 8.1%). Layer two separate blocks on top, each logged as its own line:
   - (A) Cash-like government and geopolitical terms G1-G8, sized from evidence, with G4 haircutting G1-G3.
   - (B) One subjective premium S.
   G9-G11 are scenarios and constraints, not values. K1 and K2 are counter-terms, shown as sensitivities.

2. Enter (A) at plan level.
   - G1 and G2 add PV-2026 amounts to every column of each fps plan; G1 differs between Renton and new-sites plans.
   - G5 charges an exit cost to Do Nothing and the Re-engine-only plans. This is mechanically the same as +X on fps plans.
   - G3 is a bill cut through thresholds.values() (k = 1 - c), in a scenario column only.
   - Re-run decide() under all four readings, and report whether (A) alone flips the decision.
   - Result at base values: it never does at 10.5%. At 8.1% only the high case does. Base (A) for the flipping plan, in PV-2026: about $1.0B in 2030, $0.5B in 2035, $0.25B in 2045 and $0.2B in 2050 at 10.5%; $1.2B, $0.7B, $0.4B and $0.3B at 8.1%.

3. Solve for S.
   - S_flip is the smallest S that, added to every fps plan (solo and paired) in every column, makes decide() launch. It must go into the values, not only into the CEO's allowance: H8 as coded never rescues an fps that is behind (at 10.5% the premium reading needs the same S as the rule in every round).
   - S_residual = S_flip with (A) included.
   - Report both in PV-2026 and in decision-year money: x(1+r)^(t-2026), constant 2026 dollars.
   - Note the comparator. In 2030 the fps must beat the 787 Re-engine alone (+$3.30B), not only Do Nothing. S_flip = 1 + 3.30 + 1.80 = $6.10B PV-2026, against $4.99B if only Do Nothing mattered; the extra $1.1B comes from the CEO picking the Re-engine, which the Board then vetoes. From 2035 on, S_flip = the fps's gap to Do Nothing + $1B.

4. Results (franchise.json base point; my re-implementation of decide() reproduces 4,610 of 4,610 stored decisions). Base view, full terms, rule reading:

At 10.5%:

| Round | S_flip (PV-2026 / decision-year $) | S_residual after base (A) (PV-2026 / decision-year $) |
|---|---|---|
| 2030 | $6.10B / $9.1B | $5.09B / $7.6B |
| 2035 | $4.54B / $11.2B | $4.04B / $9.9B |
| 2045 | $3.26B / $21.7B | $3.00B / $20.0B |
| 2050 | $2.48B / $27.2B | $2.28B / $25.0B |

At 8.1%:

| Round | S_flip (PV-2026 / decision-year $) | S_residual after base (A) (decision-year $) |
|---|---|---|
| 2030 | $1.38B / $1.9B | $0.27B |
| 2035 | $3.72B rule, $2.75B premium / $7.5B and $5.6B | $6.1B rule, $4.2B premium |
| 2045 | $4.56B / $20.1B | $18.3B |

Other cases:
- High franchise terms plus high (A), at 10.5%: S_residual $1.5B (2030), $1.8B (2035), $6.5B (2045), $7.4B (2050), in decision-year money.
- Low franchise terms, 10.5%, 2030: $11.6B.

5. Compare S_residual with the revealed-premium ladder (2026 dollars, CPI-deflated):

| Rung | Amount | Episodes |
|---|---|---|
| Zero | $0 | segments, China upside, Embraer when cash was tight |
| Clean ex ante | $0.9B | T-X and MQ-25 |
| Base | about $2B | the H8 cap; the Washington repeal at $1.1-3.2B; the 747-8 at $3.1B |
| Political, ex post | $3.2B | VC-25B |
| Upper bound | $6.3B | 737 workforce, mostly ordinary NPV |

Verdict rule:
- Credible: S_residual at or below $2B and the rating buffer not binding.
- Contested: between $2B and $6.3B.
- Not credible: above $6.3B.

Outcome:
- At 10.5%: not credible in any round at base. Credible only in 2030 and 2035 if both the franchise terms and the cash-like terms are at their high values.
- At 8.1%: credible in 2030, so politics and brand can tip the decision. Contested in 2035 (premium reading). Not credible in 2045 and 2050.
- Even the upper rung ($6.3B) does not close the 2030 gap at 10.5% ($7.6B). Scaling T-X and MQ-25 by contract value (about $4B on a $60B bill) does not close it either.

6. Fix the units of H8 and the Board's tests. The game states them in PV-2026. In 2050, $2B PV-2026 is $22B of 2050 money. Without the fix, a '$2B' soft premium would almost rescue the 2050 launch in the high case (S_flip $1.57B, below $2B).
   - State H8 and the other dollar tests in decision-year money (divide by (1+r)^(t-2026)).
   - With all tests deflated, S_flip changes little: $5.77B PV-2026 ($8.6B) in 2030 and $1.72B ($18.8B) in 2050 at 10.5%.
   - The S cap is shared with the objective premium (objectives.md line 113): one budget.

7. Decide the rate question first. Whether 10.5% is a real or a nominal rate moves S_flip from $9.1B to $1.9B in 2030, more than any evidence-supported political term does.

8. 'Never exit the core', if adopted, should be a hard rule with a logged cost, like H1, applied only at the last round that avoids a product gap (2050 here).
   - Its cost against the CEO's pick (decision sweep's numbers): about $1.4B PV-2026 in 2050, which is about $15B in 2050 money. In 2030 the cost is $5.1B PV-2026, about $7.6B in 2030 money.
   - Paying it early costs less in decision-year money but more in PV-2026. Boeing's record (jobs buy delay; 'not any time near') points to the late, point-of-no-return form.

9. Log line for each round: "S_flip a (PV26) / b (decision $); cash-like c (G1 .., G2 .., G5 ..); S_residual d; ladder rung e; verdict; H8 used f of $2B (decision $)".

10. Scenarios, not values:
   - G3: Washington launch support with equity strings.
   - G9: COMAC uncapped; G5's p raised to 0.5.
   - A Washington penalty column, if wanted, uniform across columns.
   - China at 0%, 10% and 20% of fps demand (G8), with announced orders discounted 40-50% until they are firm.
   - Brazil and Embraer only as the cap on the JV variant's capex share (G10).

They come from memory and from the six sweeps. Check them before publishing.
The CPI-U deflators are annual averages from memory; 2025 (about 322) and 2026 (about 330) are estimates. Conversions to 2026 dollars could be off by about 2-3%.

Many web facts in the sweeps rest on search excerpts, because trade.gov, sec.gov, boeing.com, axios.com and other hosts blocked fetching. Several older facts are labelled 'from memory' in the sweeps: the Washington 2003 package, the WTO DS353 totals, the Super Hornet cancellation in Canada, the CARES $17B and the 2025 equity stakes.
The sizes of G1-G8 are my inferences from precedents. G5 rests on assumptions, not evidence: defence revenue of about $27B, an 8% margin, 20% of profit at risk, and p = 0.2.

S_flip comes from the base-point values in franchise.json, with decide() re-implemented in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-aero-engine-gameboard/95fa875c-ca9d-5564-a6e5-4c9b461d7e56/scratchpad/geo/design/scripts/design.py. It reproduces 4,610 of the 4,610 stored decisions. Rival moves are held as the game played them.
S is uniform across columns. Political salience is probably higher when Airbus launches NGSA or COMAC gains Western certification. A column-weighted S would change the downside test only slightly.

Only T-X and MQ-25 is a clean ex-ante revealed premium. VC-25B, KC-46 and the 747-8 are ex-post losses on contracts or launched programmes, and the 737 workforce payment is mostly ordinary NPV. The ladder therefore overstates what Boeing chooses to pay up front.

The Board's time horizon is 3 out of 5 and long-term pay rests on 3-year free cash flow (board.md; BG-0026). A premium for effects after 2045 has little purchase on this Board unless the rating is secure.

Under Do Nothing the political cost lands in 2045-60, so at 10.5% it is heavily discounted. Airbus's Mobile lines (two A320, one A220, more than 2,000 staff) mean not all final-assembly jobs would leave the US.
No US official or member of Congress was found demanding a 737 successor. That may be a gap in the searches rather than a true absence.

problems.item: revealed_premiums > Washington tax-preference repeal (2020): what_it_bought
problems.problem: The design says the repeal bought 'Removal of the legal basis for the EU's $3.99B-a-year WTO retaliation'. Boeing's own 10-K shows the EU was authorised and imposed 15% tariffs on Boeing aircraft after the repeal. The tariff relief came only with the June 2021 truce. So the repeal did not buy trade access when it was made, and its use as a 'revealed geopolitical premium paid for trade access' (base rung, and the G4 justification) misstates the outcome. The design also leaves out the repeal's snapback clause, so 'forgone to 2040' may overstate the amount.
problems.evidence: 10-K FY2020 p.1369 (B-1761): 'In October 2020, the WTO authorized the EU to impose approximately $3.99 billion in annual tariffs ... in connection with a tax incentive used by Boeing in Washington state that has since been repealed. The EU is currently imposing 15% tariffs on Boeing airplanes'. dc-jobs research: lawmakers repealed it in March 2020 'with a snapback clause'; truce June 2021 (B-1825 p.683).
problems.fix: Restate what it bought: 'a legal position in the WTO dispute; the EU tariffs stayed until the June 2021 truce'. Label the $1.1-3.2B as an upper bound because of the snapback. Keep it out of the base rung, or mark its comparability as low.

problems.fix: Lead with the 27 Oct 2026 Ortberg quote, which postdates every event listed. Present the Malave quote as the March 2026 baseline that the later events did not change.

problems.item: S (and G5) added to the risk-case column, so a non-cash premium relaxes the Board's rating test
problems.problem: The design adds S to every column, including the risk-case column that the rating test reads. The rating test is a balance-sheet test, and a brand or identity premium does not make spend affordable. The design's own rule says S should be zero when the rating buffer binds (the Embraer lesson), but its S_flip computation never applies that rule. When S and G5 are kept out of the rating column, no finite S launches the fps in most rounds: at base, 10.5%, in 2030, 2035 and 2045; at 8.1% in 2045 and 2050. This holds even with base (A) added. So at those points the binding constraint is the balance sheet, not the size of the premium.
problems.evidence: board/board.md line 369: 'Rating first: Veto a package whose spend the CFO memo shows would threaten the investment-grade rating, or which fails the CFO's buffer test'. Cash gap of the flipping plan to Do Nothing in the risk column, base|full (the test needs >= -2.0): at 10.5%, 2030 10-year new sites -4.05, 2035 10-year Renton -3.65, 2045 -2.31, 2050 -1.50; at 8.1%, 2030 +0.96, 2035 -1.93, 2045 -3.24, 2050 -2.51. Result with S and G5 kept out of the rating column: S_flip is None (no finite S) in 2030, 2035 and 2045 at 10.5% with base (A), and in 2030 and 2035 even with high (A). Only 2050 is finite ($2.28B PV-2026). At 8.1%: None in 2045 and 2050. The design's three 'credible' cases survive (rating margins -1.61, -1.66, +0.96). Scripts: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-aero-engine-gameboard/95fa875c-ca9d-5564-a6e5-4c9b461d7e56/scratchpad/geo/check-logic/check.py, check2.py and out1.txt. My re-implementation reproduces the design's S_flip values exactly. Confidence: high.
problems.fix: Split the test: add S and G5 to every column for the CEO's pick, the business case and the downside test, but run the rating test on cash values only (game, franchise terms, G1-G3 cash). Report 'no finite S; rating binds' where that happens, and say plainly that only cash (a G3 bill cut or the rate question) can move those rounds.

problems.item: S solved round by round treats every round without a launch as a permanent exit (option to launch later ignored)
problems.problem: Each round's brief values Do Nothing as never launching, but the game offers later rounds. A 'never exit the core' premium is met by a launch in any round up to 2050, so between 'launch now' and 'launch later' S cancels. Only the point of no return (2050) should carry S. In PV-2026 at 10.5%, the cost of staying in falls the longer Boeing waits, so the 2030-2045 S values do not answer 'what premium stops an exit'. At 8.1% in 2030, S is not about exit at all: the solo fps already passes every Board test on cash, and what blocks it is the 787 Re-engine through the CEO's 'doing less' rule. Yet the design reads that case as 'politics and brand can tip the decision'. The design itself says the premium 'bites at the point of no return' (its item 8), but its verdicts (item 5) are per round.
problems.evidence: Best solo fps against Do Nothing in the CEO's column, base|full|10.5%, PV-2026: 2030 -3.99, 2035 -3.54, 2045 -2.25, 2050 -1.47. At 8.1% in 2030 the 10-year new sites (no S) has e +1.05, smallest column item +0.80 and risk gap +0.96, so it passes the business-case, downside and rating tests. The Re-engine scores +5.33 and is the CEO's pick. The game path to 2050 is the waiting path: the Re-engine is still on offer in 2050 (e +0.24), so it was never launched. Caveat: rival states differ by round, so the comparison across rounds is indicative. Confidence: high on the mechanics, medium on the size.
problems.fix: Apply S only in the last round that avoids a product gap (2050), or as S x P(no later launch | no launch now) in earlier rounds. Re-label the 2030 result at 8.1% as 'fps against the 787 Re-engine' (a choice between programmes), not as a political or exit premium. G5 has the same problem, because it charges Do Nothing an exit cost in rounds where exit is not yet final.

problems.item: The 2030 S_flip is an artefact of the decision process: at the design's own S_flip, Boeing launches a plan worth less than the Re-engine it gives up
problems.problem: In 2030 the S that flips the decision makes the CEO pick the fps + Re-engine pair. The Board then vetoes the Re-engine beside the fps, and the solo fps goes ahead. Even counting S, that solo plan is worth less than the Re-engine alone, which the CEO would otherwise have chosen. If the CEO anticipates the veto, the 2030 S_flip rises sharply, and the 8.1% case moves from 'credible' to 'contested'. The design's explanation ('the extra $1.1B comes from the CEO picking the Re-engine, which the Board then vetoes') is also wrong: the Board vetoes the Re-engine beside the fps, not the Re-engine alone.
problems.evidence: At S = 6.10 (base|full|10.5%) the launched 10-year new sites has e +2.11 including S, against the Re-engine alone at +3.30. At 8.1%, S = 1.38 gives +2.43 against +5.33. With the CEO anticipating the Board, S_flip is $8.30B PV-2026 ($12.4B in 2030 money) at 10.5% and $4.20B (7-year at Renton; $5.7B in 2030 money) at 8.1%, against the design's 6.10 and 1.38. Just below S_flip the pairs fail the business case against the Re-engine by $0.01B (0.993 against the 1.0 test). Script: check.py, section 1. Confidence: high.
problems.fix: Report the 2030 S_flip as a range across readings: the rule reading as stored, and a 'CEO anticipates Board' reading. Note that at the low end the launch is dominated even including S. With the anticipating reading, the 8.1% verdict for 2030 becomes 'contested' (S_residual about $3.0B PV-2026 after base (A)).

problems.item: Revealed-premium ladder: most rungs are not premiums over NPV, and the rest are not on the same basis as S
problems.problem:
S must exclude C1 (continuing value) and every cash term. Most rungs fail one of those tests:
- T-X and MQ-25 (the 'clean ex-ante' base rung) bought franchise follow-on value. That is the same logic C1 already credits to the fps, so it double counts C1.
- The 747-8 charges were sunk reach-forward losses on aircraft already contracted, not a payment to keep going.
- The 737 workforce rung is mostly ordinary NPV, as the design itself says, yet it sets the line between 'contested' and 'not credible'.
- The Washington repeal was a cash trade: tax relief given up to remove 15% EU tariffs on Boeing aircraft.
- VC-25B is ex post and undiscounted.
- H8 is itself an inference in profile.md, so using it as a rung is circular.
The evidence therefore supports an S close to zero beyond cash, not a base of $0.9-2.0B.
problems.evidence: B-1458 (FQ3 2018, p.1146): 'position ourselves to capture significant future market opportunity', with numbers 'tx_market_aircraft 2600, tx_opportunity_usd_bn 40'. B-1761 (10-K FY2020 p.1369): '15% tariffs on Boeing airplanes' over the Washington incentive. profile.md line 31: H8 '$2B for a soft doctrine choice (inference)'. VC-25B: $3.16B undiscounted in 2026 dollars, but $2.10B (10.5%) to $2.29B (8.1%) as PV at the 2018 decision; the ex-ante premium is unknown and probably smaller. Confidence: high that the rungs are not comparable; medium on the sizes.
problems.fix: Make the zero rung the evidence-based base. Keep T-X only as a sensitivity, and net of C1. Restate every rung as an ex-ante PV at its own decision date, in constant 2026 dollars. Drop the 747-8, the 737 workforce and the Washington repeal as evidence for S. Present the $2B cap as a game rule, not as evidence. Replace the $2B and $6.3B verdict bands with: S at about 0-0.9B is supported; anything above is a judgement call that must be logged as such.

problems.item: Premium reading stacks S on top of the H8 allowance, although the design says the two share one $2B budget
problems.problem: The premium reading's lower S_flip at 8.1% comes from using H8 headroom on top of S. objectives.md line 113 says the objective premium and any doctrine premium share one cap. Measured against that shared budget, the premium reading gives no relief over the rule reading.
problems.evidence: 2035 at 8.1%: S_flip(premium) $2.75B plus $0.93B of H8 used gives $3.68B, against the rule reading's $3.715B. 2045 at 8.1%: $4.11B plus $0.59B gives $4.70B, against $4.555B. The design's 'Contested in 2035 (premium reading)' figure of $4.2B in 2035 money becomes about $6.1B. Script: check.py (h8_used). Confidence: high.
problems.fix: Report S plus the H8 headroom used as the premium reading's total, or solve S with H8 set to (2 - S).

problems.item: Co-funding (G2, the capex-grant part of G1, and G3) enters on a different basis from the game's bill, and G3 is compared with thresholds solved for a different case
problems.problem: The game charges the whole fps bill at entry into service and marks it up by the debt penalty. The design instead adds G2 and G1 grants as flat amounts discounted from the decision year, which over-credits them. The stored bill-cut thresholds hold only when no other term is on. They also flip a different plan from S: the 7-year at Renton, whose bill is bigger, rather than the 10-year at new sites.
problems.evidence: model.true_cost: debt $45B, EV $130B, alpha 0.3. The marginal markup is 0.591 on the 10-year bill and 0.644 on the 7-year. Through k, $1 of co-funding at the decision year is worth 0.59 (10-year, 10.5%), 0.73 (10-year, 8.1%), 0.82 (7-year, 10.5%) or 0.95 (7-year, 8.1%) of the design's flat add. The stored cut at base|full|10.5% (rule) is 26.0%, with plan_at_cut '7-year at Renton', while S flips the '10-year, new sites'. Script: check.py, section 5. Confidence: high.
problems.fix: Enter G2, the G1 capex grants and G3 through thresholds.values(k = 1 - c); enter tax relief through the margin. Re-solve the cut with (A) and S switched on instead of reading the stored threshold.

problems.item: G1 and G4 ranges: the new-sites incentive equals the game's whole new-site capex, and the main precedent was fully reversed
problems.problem: The base G1 for new sites, in PV-2026, about equals all the new-site capex the game charges, and the high case is about twice it. The Washington 2013 package, the anchor for G1, was repealed in 2020 at Boeing's own request. That happened before its extension years (to 2040) began, so its realised value was about zero. Boeing has also pledged that all future support should be on market terms. A base haircut of h = 0.25 cannot be defended on that record.
problems.evidence: G1 new sites base in PV-2026 is 0.75 in 2030, 0.46 in 2035, 0.17 in 2045 and 0.10 in 2050. The game's $3.0B of new-site capex (supply_demand.json renton_saving_b, charged at entry into service) is 0.74, 0.45, 0.17 and 0.10 in PV-2026. B-1761: the incentive 'has since been repealed'. B-1825: 'all future government support ... must be provided on market terms. We will fully support'. The extension's 2024 start is from memory: the web-search budget was exhausted. Verdict effect: none at 10.5%. At 8.1% in 2030, G1 is about $0.82B of the $1.18B of (A); removing it raises S_residual to about $1.0B PV-2026, still within $2B. Confidence: medium.
problems.fix: Make h = 0.5 or more the base, or move G1's low case to base. Cap the capex-grant part of G1 at the game's new-site capex. Note that renewing the IAM clause removes the site auction altogether.

problems.item: G5 timing and type: a fixed 2045-64 stream in every round, past years charged in 2050, and goodwill counted as cash
problems.problem: In the 2050 round, the years 2045-49 of G5 are already in the past, so no 2050 launch can avoid them, yet G5 still charges them. G5 is lost goodwill, not cash, so it should not enter the rating test. L uses the 8% target margin while actual defence (BDS) margins are -22.6% (2024) and 3.1% (Q1 2026). The Ex-Im goodwill on widebody campaigns overlaps C4.
problems.evidence: Avoidable PV-2026 in the 2050 round: $0.065B against the design's $0.109B at 10.5%, and $0.124B against $0.194B at 8.1% (check.py, section 6). The design's own sources give the BDS margins. Effect on the decision: negligible. Confidence: high on the mechanics.
problems.fix: Start the stream at max(t_exit, decision year), leave G5 out of the rating column, size L at a range of realised margins, and keep Ex-Im support for widebody campaigns out of L.

problems.item: K2 (lower cost of capital after exit) is a valuation error, not a counter-term
problems.problem: When Boeing exits a high-beta segment, its blended WACC falls, but that does not create value. A sum-of-parts valuation already discounts each business at its own rate, so nothing is revalued by the exit, and K2 should be zero. Its low case of -$1.0B is arbitrary: applied to all remaining cash flows, a blended-rate change could be tens of billions, which shows the method is wrong.
problems.evidence: In the design, K2 rests on a beta comparison from a search excerpt (Lockheed about 0.1-0.3 against Boeing about 1.2-1.4). Confidence: medium.
problems.fix: Remove K2, or replace it with a segment-specific rate for the fps's own cash flows. That is the existing 10.5% versus 8.1% question.

problems.item: Verdict tables mix test units and contain wording errors
problems.problem: Points 4 and 5 report S_flip with the Board's tests in PV-2026, while point 6 recommends stating them in decision-year money. The verdicts should use one convention. 'Almost rescue' is wrong, because $1.57B is below $2B, so a $2B premium would rescue the launch. 'From 2035 on, S_flip = gap + $1B' holds only at 10.5%.
problems.fix: Pick one convention for the verdict, preferably the deflated tests if the fix is recommended, and show the other as a sensitivity. Correct the two sentences.

problems.item: S's definition overlaps G5, and the ladder's high rung is a G5-type political payment
problems.problem: S's 'standing as national champion and last US airliner maker' is the same channel as G5 (goodwill in Washington). VC-25B, which bought the White House relationship, is also a G5-type payment. Comparing S_residual (with G5 already taken out) against a ladder topped by VC-25B counts the political channel twice.
problems.evidence: Design: S what_it_captures; the VC-25B 'what_it_bought'; G5 what_it_captures. Confidence: medium.
problems.fix: Limit S to identity, engineering and talent value not covered by C3, and treat VC-25B as calibration for G5 (p x L), not as a rung for S.
